In this paper, we conduct a detailed investigation on how to enhance LLMs to produce more logically consistent answers. Specifically, we first investigate the existing issues of current LLMs in doing some complex reasoning tasks (e.g., event relation extraction and deductive reasoning). Then, we study multiple strategies to obtain and utilize logic for LLMs, including generative-based, retrieval- based, and pre training-based approaches. Based on our approach, we also contribute a synthesized dataset ( LLM-LR ) involving multi- hop reasoning for evaluation and pre-training. We show that LLMs are not logically consistent reasoners, but their performance could be improved if we explicitly teach them the logical constraints. Comprehensive quantitative and qualitative analyses have been conducted to further provide insights.

There also have been some recent explorations on how to lever- age the power of LLMs on event-related information extraction tasks [ 12 ,  27 ,  43 ]. To the best of our knowledge, however, our work is the first to (1) design elaborate experiments to evaluate the per- formance of LLMs on the ERE task, and (2) analyze the logical reasoning abilities of LLMs using ERE as an intermediate task.

We introduce the Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Un- der standing and Reasoning ( MMMU ) benchmark, a novel benchmark meticulously curated to assess the expert-level multimodal understanding capability of foundation models across a broad scope of tasks. Covering 30 subjects across 6 disciplines, including Art, Business, Health & Medicine, Science, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engi- neering, and over 183 subfields. The detailed subject cover- age and statistics are detailed in  Figure 3 . The questions in our benchmark were manually collected by a team of 50 college students (including coauthors) from various dis- ciplines and subjects, drawing from online sources, text- books, and lecture materials.

How to create benchmarks for measuring Expert AGI? Since the definition is based on comparison with  skilled adults , a natural starting point is college-level exams for different disciplines, because those are designed to evalu- ate  skilled adults  specialized in each discipline. This strat- egy has been successfully adopted in benchmarks such as MMLU [ 19 ] and AGIEval [ 69 ], but only text-based ques- tions are considered, while human experts are capable of solving multimodal problems. Meanwhile, large multi- modal models (LMMs) that can understand both text and images have been making a major stride towards more gen- eral AI [ 8 ,  14 ,  27 ,  34 ,  58 ]. These LMMs have consistently excelled in existing multimodal benchmarks [ 3 ,  18 ,  25 ,  31 , 36 ,  50 ,  61 ,  63 ]. For instance,   $\mathbf{\mathrm{CogVLM}}$   [ 55 ] achieves  $85\%$  on VQA-v2 [ 18 ],  $92\%$   on ScienceQA-IMG [ 39 ], and    $93\%$  on RefCOCO [ 23 ]. However, most existing multimodal benchmarks focus on commonsense/daily knowledge rather than expert-level domain knowledge and advanced reason- ing. The closest one to our goal is ScienceQA [ 39 ]. While it covers diverse disciplines ( breadth ), the majority of the questions are at the elementary to the middle school level, thus falling short in  depth  for benchmarking Expert AGI.

To this end, we introduce  MMMU : a comprehensive benchmark designed for college-level multi-discipline mul- timodal understanding and reasoning. It features problems sourced from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks span- ning six common disciplines: Art & Design, Business, Sci- ence, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engineering.  MMMU  consists of  11 . 5 K carefully selected multimodal questions, which cover  30  diverse sub- jects and  183  subfields, thus meeting the  breadth  goal. Moreover, many problems within  MMMU  require expert-level reasoning, such as applying “Fourier Transform” or “Equi- librium Theory” to derive the solution, thus meeting the depth  goal.  MMMU  also presents two unique challenges ab- sent in current benchmarks ( Figure 1 ). Firstly, it covers di- verse image formats, from visual scenes like photographs and paintings to diagrams and tables, testing the perceptual capabilities of LMMs. Secondly,  MMMU  features interleaved text-image inputs. A model needs to jointly understand the images and text, which often requires recalling deep subject knowledge, and conducting complex reasoning based on the understanding and knowledge to reach a solution.

We introduce  MMMU : a new benchmark designed to eval- uate multimodal models on massive multi-discipline tasks demanding college-level subject knowledge and deliberate reasoning. MMMU  includes   $l l.5K$   meticulously collected multimodal questions from college exams, quizzes, and text- books, covering six core disciplines: Art & Design, Busi- ness, Science, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engineering. These questions span 30 subjects and 183 subfields, comprising 30 highly het- erogeneous image types, such as charts, diagrams, maps, tables, music sheets, and chemical structures. Unlike ex- isting benchmarks,  MMMU  focuses on advanced perception and reasoning with domain-specific knowledge, challenging models to perform tasks akin to those faced by experts. The evaluation of 14 open-source LMMs as well as the propri- etary GPT-4V(ision) and Gemini highlights the substantial challenges posed by  MMMU . Even the advanced GPT-4V and Gemini Ultra only achieve accuracies of   $56\%$   and  $59\%$   re- spectively, indicating significant room for improvement. We believe  MMMU  will stimulate the community to build next- generation multimodal foundation models towards expert artificial general intelligence.

We introduce the Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Un- der standing and Reasoning ( MMMU ) benchmark, a novel benchmark meticulously curated to assess the expert-level multimodal understanding capability of foundation models across a broad scope of tasks. question: How does the distribution of questions across different disciplines in the MMMU dataset relate to the types and formats of questions used?
answer:
The MMMU dataset is designed to cover a broad range of disciplines, subjects, and subfields, with a focus on college-level difficulty and multimodal reasoning. The distribution of questions across these disciplines is carefully curated to reflect the diversity and complexity of expert-level knowledge required for advanced multimodal understanding.

### Distribution Across Disciplines:
The dataset spans six core disciplines: **Art & Design**, **Business**, **Science**, **Health & Medicine**, **Humanities & Social Science**, and **Tech & Engineering**. These disciplines are selected based on their relevance to multimodal reasoning and the availability of visual or textual content that can be used to create challenging questions. Each discipline contributes to the overall goal of testing a model's ability to integrate and synthesize information from diverse sources.

### Types and Formats of Questions:
The questions in the MMMU dataset are primarily **multiple-choice** (94.03%), with a smaller portion being **open-ended** (5.97%). This reflects the need for both structured evaluation (via multiple-choice) and the ability to assess deeper reasoning through open-ended questions. The inclusion of both formats ensures that models are tested not only on their ability to recall specific facts but also on their capacity for nuanced reasoning and synthesis.

### Image Types and Question Formats:
The dataset includes a high percentage of questions that incorporate images (97.52%), indicating a strong emphasis on multimodal reasoning. Images are often placed at the beginning (17.81%) or in the middle (36.92%) of the question, requiring models to process visual information alongside textual data. This integration of image types aligns with the dataset's goal of evaluating models' ability to handle complex, real-world scenarios where visual and textual information must be combined.

### Difficulty Levels:
The questions are categorized into three difficulty levels: **Easy (28%)**, **Medium (45%)**, and **Hard (27%)**. This distribution ensures that the dataset can test models at various levels of proficiency, from basic comprehension to advanced reasoning. The inclusion of harder questions, such as those requiring expert-level knowledge (e.g., applying "Fourier Transform" or "Equilibrium Theory"), further challenges models to demonstrate deep subject knowledge and deliberate reasoning.

### Conclusion:
The distribution of questions across disciplines in the MMMU dataset is closely tied to the types and formats of questions used. By covering a wide range of subjects and subfields, the dataset ensures that models are tested on their ability to handle diverse and complex multimodal reasoning tasks. The combination of multiple-choice and open-ended questions, along with the frequent use of images, reflects the dataset's goal of evaluating advanced multimodal understanding and reasoning capabilities. This comprehensive approach makes the MMMU benchmark a valuable tool for assessing the progress of multimodal models toward Expert AGI.

question: How does the MMMU benchmark compare to other datasets in terms of reasoning depth and knowledge breadth, and what are its characteristics in terms of question types and distribution across disciplines?
answer:
The MMMU benchmark stands out for its focus on reasoning depth and knowledge breadth, particularly in the context of multimodal understanding. It is designed to evaluate models' ability to handle complex, college-level tasks that require both subject-specific knowledge and deliberate reasoning across multiple modalities.

### Comparison to Other Datasets:
Compared to other datasets like OK-VQA, AOK-VQA, or WebQA, which primarily test visual question answering or knowledge base queries, MMMU introduces a higher level of complexity. While those datasets often involve simpler reasoning or rely on external knowledge bases, MMMU emphasizes **multimodal reasoning** that requires integrating information from text, images, and other modalities. This makes it more challenging and closer to real-world problem-solving scenarios.

Moreover, MMMU surpasses datasets like MMLU (which focuses on language understanding) by incorporating **visual and multimodal components**, making it more suitable for evaluating models that need to reason across different types of data.

### Characteristics of Question Types and Distribution:
1. **Question Types**: 
   - The questions in MMMU are carefully curated to demand **deep reasoning** and **subject knowledge**. They are not just simple fact-based queries but require models to perform multi-step reasoning, integrate information from various sources, and apply knowledge in nuanced ways.
   - These questions span a wide range of formats, including multiple-choice, open-ended, and those requiring abstract reasoning.

2. **Distribution Across Disciplines**:
   - MMMU covers six core disciplines: **Art & Design, Business, Science, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engineering**.
   - Within these disciplines, the benchmark includes 30 subjects and 183 subfields, ensuring a broad and diverse coverage of college-level topics.
   - The dataset is meticulously constructed to avoid biases and ensure a balanced distribution of questions across disciplines, with a focus on areas where multimodal reasoning is most critical.

3. **Annotator Involvement**:
   - The questions were collected by university students specializing in relevant fields, ensuring high-quality and domain-specific content. This approach also helps maintain the integrity of the dataset by adhering to copyright and licensing regulations.

### Summary:
In summary, MMMU distinguishes itself by combining **reasoning depth** and **knowledge breadth** in a way that challenges models to perform at a higher level of sophistication. Its focus on multimodal reasoning, coupled with a broad and balanced distribution of questions across disciplines, makes it a valuable benchmark for evaluating the next generation of multimodal foundation models. Despite its advancements, the benchmark highlights that there is still significant room for improvement, especially in domains involving complex visual input and heavy reasoning.

question: How does the MMMU benchmark compare to other benchmarks in terms of reasoning depth, knowledge breadth, and the variety of image types used?
answer:
The MMMU benchmark stands out compared to other benchmarks due to its focus on reasoning depth, knowledge breadth, and the variety of image types used. Unlike many existing benchmarks that primarily test basic visual perception or relatively simple multimodal reasoning tasks, MMMU requires models to demonstrate expert-level domain knowledge and deliberate reasoning across a wide range of subjects. This includes disciplines such as Art & Design, Business, Science, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Technology & Engineering, covering 30 subjects and 183 subfields.

In terms of reasoning depth, MMMU challenges models to go beyond simple fact extraction or basic cross-modal reasoning. Instead, it demands complex reasoning that integrates both visual and textual information, often requiring an understanding of subject-specific knowledge. For example, questions may involve interpreting intricate visual data, such as diagrams, charts, or images from textbooks, and combining this with deep subject knowledge to derive solutions.

Regarding knowledge breadth, MMMU is designed to evaluate models on a vast array of topics, ensuring that they can handle diverse and interdisciplinary problems. This is achieved by collecting questions from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks, which reflect the complexity and depth of real-world academic challenges. The benchmark thus tests not only a model's ability to process various heterogeneous image types but also its capacity to reason with subject-specific knowledge.

In terms of image variety, MMMU incorporates a wide range of image types, including those from scientific papers, medical illustrations, engineering diagrams, and artistic designs. This diversity ensures that models are tested on their ability to handle different modalities and interpret complex visual information accurately.

Overall, MMMU represents a significant advancement in evaluating multimodal models, as it pushes the boundaries of what these models can achieve in terms of reasoning depth, knowledge breadth, and image type variety. While other benchmarks have made progress in specific areas, MMMU provides a more holistic assessment of a model's capabilities in handling complex, real-world multimodal tasks.

### Performance Across Difficulty Levels and Image Types

### Key Errors Encountered by GPT-4V

2. **Object Localization and Counting**:
   - In tasks involving object localization and counting, GPT-4V might struggle with identifying and counting objects in cluttered or overlapping scenes, leading to inaccuracies.

3. **Multimodal Knowledge and Commonsense Reasoning**:
   - GPT-4V may face challenges in integrating multimodal knowledge and applying commonsense reasoning. This can result in errors when the model needs to understand the context and relationships between different types of information presented in both text and images.

5. **Multilingual Scenarios**:
   - In multilingual scenarios, GPT-4V might encounter difficulties in comprehending and generating accurate descriptions, particularly when dealing with less common languages or dialects.

6. **Coding Proficiency with Visual Information**:
   - Tasks requiring coding proficiency with visual information, such as performing operations based on selected examples, may pose challenges for GPT-4V, leading to potential errors in code generation or execution.

question: Which evaluation frameworks focus on both retrieval and generation quality, and what metrics and aspects do they use?
answer:
The evaluation frameworks that focus on both retrieval and generation quality often aim to address the unique challenges of dialogue systems, where context plays a significant role in determining appropriate responses. One such framework is "RetrieveNReﬁne+," which combines retrieval and generation models to improve dialogue performance. This approach retrieves relevant responses and then refines them to ensure they are contextually appropriate and coherent.

In terms of metrics, these frameworks typically use a combination of automated metrics and human evaluations. Automated metrics like BLEU or chrF++ are borrowed from machine translation tasks but may not fully capture the nuances of dialogue. Human evaluations are crucial here because they provide insights into the fluency, coherence, and relevance of the generated responses, which are harder to assess with automated metrics alone.

Additionally, some frameworks, like the one presented in Document 4, introduce new metrics such as COMET1, which aim to better correlate with human judgment at the segment level. These metrics are designed to be more robust and capable of differentiating between high-performing systems, providing a more accurate assessment of dialogue quality.

Overall, these evaluation frameworks strive to balance the strengths of retrieval and generation models while using a mix of automated and human-centric metrics to ensure comprehensive assessment of dialogue systems.
reference_answer_short: RGB, RAGAS, ARES, TruLens, and CRUD focus on both retrieval and generation quality, using metrics like Accuracy, EM, Cosine Similarity, and BLEU, and aspects such as Context Relevance, Faithfulness, and Noise Robustness.
reference_answers:
The evaluation of frameworks focusing on both retrieval and generation quality is critical in understanding their efficiency and applicability. Several frameworks have been identified to address these dual targets, as illustrated in the following analysis.

![Evaluation Framework Overview](image2)

### Frameworks and their Aspects & Metrics:

1. **RGB (Retrieval and Generation Quality)**
   - **Aspects**: Noise Robustness, Negative Rejection, Information Integration, Counterfactual Robustness.
   - **Metrics**: Utilizes Accuracy and EM (Exact Match) to gauge retrieval and generation quality.

2. **RAGAS (Retrieval and Generation Quality)**
   - **Aspects**: Context Relevance, Faithfulness, Answer Relevance.
   - **Metrics**: Employs Cosine Similarity, although specific metrics for Context Relevance and Faithfulness are unspecified.

3. **ARES (Retrieval and Generation Quality)**
   - **Aspects**: Context Relevance, Faithfulness, Answer Relevance.
   - **Metrics**: Relies on Accuracy across all aspects to measure the quality of both retrieval and generation.

4. **TruLens (Retrieval and Generation Quality)**
   - **Aspects**: Context Relevance, Faithfulness, Answer Relevance.
   - **Metrics**: Although metrics are unspecified in the table, they are structured similarly to RAGAS.

5. **CRUD (Retrieval and Generation Quality)**
   - **Aspects**: Creative Generation, Knowledge-intensive QA, Error Correction, Summarization.
   - **Metrics**: Uses BLEU, ROUGE-L, BertScore, and RAGQuestEval to evaluate the quality.

![Metrics and Aspects](image5)

question: What are the key evaluation aspects and metrics used for assessing RAG's retrieval and generation quality, and how do these aspects differ across various evaluation frameworks?
answer:
The evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models focuses on two primary aspects: **retrieval quality** and **generation quality**, each assessed using specific metrics that vary across different frameworks. Below is a comprehensive overview of these evaluation aspects and metrics:

### 1. **Retrieval Quality**
   - **Context Relevance**: This evaluates how precise and specific the retrieved context is, ensuring it aligns with the query while minimizing extraneous content. Metrics like **Hit Rate**, **Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR)**, and **Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG)** are commonly used to measure retrieval effectiveness.
   - **Noise Robustness**: This aspect assesses the model's ability to handle irrelevant or noisy data in the retrieved context. It ensures that the retrieved information remains accurate and useful despite potential noise.
   - **Negative Rejection**: This metric evaluates the model's capability to reject irrelevant or incorrect information during retrieval. It helps maintain the integrity of the retrieved context.

### 2. **Generation Quality**
   - **Answer Faithfulness**: This measures whether the generated answers remain true to the retrieved context, ensuring consistency and avoiding hallucinations.
   - **Answer Relevance**: This evaluates how well the generated answers address the query. Metrics like **Cosine Similarity** are often used to quantify relevance.
   - **Information Integration**: This aspect assesses the model's ability to synthesize and integrate information from multiple sources into coherent responses.
   - **Counterfactual Robustness**: This evaluates the model's performance under hypothetical or altered scenarios, ensuring robustness in diverse contexts.
   - **Creative Generation**: Metrics like **BLEU** and **ROUGE-L** are used to evaluate the creativity and fluency of generated text, particularly in tasks like summarization.

### Differences Across Evaluation Frameworks
Different frameworks emphasize various metrics based on their specific goals and methodologies:
- **Traditional Metrics**: Some frameworks rely on established metrics like **BLEU**, **ROUGE-L**, and **Cosine Similarity** for evaluating generation quality.
- **Customized Metrics**: Certain frameworks introduce **customized quantitative metrics** that deviate from traditional ones, tailored to specific tasks or datasets.
- **Benchmark Tools**: Frameworks may use tools like **TruLens** or **ARES** for automated evaluation, or benchmarks like **CRUD** for knowledge-intensive tasks.
- **Manual vs. Automatic Evaluation**: Some frameworks employ manual evaluation methods to assess retrieval and generation quality, while others use automatic methods for scalability.

In summary, the evaluation of RAG models involves a combination of retrieval and generation quality assessments, with metrics varying based on the framework's focus and objectives. These evaluations aim to optimize RAG models for diverse application scenarios, ensuring both accuracy and efficiency in information retrieval and generation.

question: What are the key differences between the evaluation targets and aspects of the RGB and CRUD evaluation frameworks in the context of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)?
answer:
The evaluation frameworks RGB and CRUD serve distinct purposes in assessing Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models, focusing on different targets and aspects of performance. Here's a breakdown of their key differences:

1. **Evaluation Targets**:
   - **RGB**: This framework primarily focuses on evaluating the essential abilities of RAG models, particularly in terms of retrieval quality. It emphasizes how well the model retrieves relevant information from the context.
   - **CRUD**: In contrast, CRUD is designed to evaluate a broader range of tasks, including knowledge-intensive question answering (QA), error correction, and summarization. It aims to assess the model's ability to handle complex downstream tasks effectively.

2. **Evaluation Aspects**:
   - **RGB**: The primary evaluation aspect for RGB is retrieval quality, specifically looking at negative rejection and ensuring that the retrieved context is precise and relevant. It also considers information integration accuracy during the generation phase.
   - **CRUD**: This framework evaluates multiple aspects, including retrieval quality, generation quality, and answer relevance. It places a strong emphasis on ensuring that the generated answers are faithful to the retrieved context and relevant to the query.

3. **Quantitative Metrics**:
   - **RGB**: The metrics used in RGB include Exact Match (EM) for retrieval quality and a metric called R-Rate (Reappearance Rate) for counterfactual robustness. These metrics help quantify how accurately the model retrieves and integrates information.
   - **CRUD**: CRUD employs a variety of metrics such as BLEU for creative generation, ROUGE-L for knowledge-intensive QA, and BertScore for error correction. These metrics provide a comprehensive view of the model's performance across different tasks.

In summary, while RGB is more focused on the retrieval aspect and ensuring high-quality context retrieval, CRUD takes a broader approach by evaluating the model's performance across various downstream tasks, including generation and answer relevance. Both frameworks contribute to a deeper understanding of RAG model capabilities but cater to different evaluation needs.

question: How does the Advanced RAG improve upon the Naive RAG, and what role does the Modular RAG play in enhancing retrieval-augmented generation?
answer:
Advanced RAG improves upon Naive RAG by addressing specific limitations in the retrieval-augmented generation process. While Naive RAG represents an early methodology that gained prominence shortly after the initial research momentum, it lacks specialized strategies for integrating retrieved information effectively with language models. This can lead to issues such as including irrelevant documents, which may unexpectedly increase accuracy but contradicts the assumption of reduced quality.

In contrast, Advanced RAG introduces more sophisticated techniques to enhance retrieval and processing capabilities. It focuses on optimizing the retrieval process, including indexing, query optimization, and embedding optimization. Additionally, it emphasizes post-retrieval processes, such as reranking chunks and compressing context, to ensure that the most relevant information is integrated effectively with the query.

Modular RAG builds upon the principles of both Advanced and Naive RAG, representing a refined and progressive approach within the RAG family. It introduces new modules, such as the Search module, which adapts to specialized retrieval needs. These additional components enhance the system's ability to handle knowledge-intensive tasks and improve the overall integration of retrieved information with language models. Modular RAG also showcases dynamic use of module outputs to bolster another module’s functionality, illustrating a sophisticated understanding of enhancing module synergy.

In summary, Advanced RAG addresses the shortcomings of Naive RAG by introducing optimized retrieval and post-retrieval processes, while Modular RAG further refines these techniques by adding specialized components and improving the integration of retrieval with language models. Together, these advancements contribute to more effective and efficient retrieval-augmented generation systems.

question: How do the Naive, Advanced, and Modular RAG frameworks differ in their approach to handling document retrieval and query processing?
answer:
The Naive, Advanced, and Modular RAG frameworks represent different stages of evolution in handling document retrieval and query processing, each addressing specific limitations and enhancing performance in distinct ways.

1. **Naive RAG**: This is the earliest methodology in the RAG family. It primarily focuses on retrieving relevant document chunks based on semantic similarity to the user's query. The process involves indexing documents into chunks, encoding them into vectors, and storing them in a vector database. When a query is received, it is transformed into a vector representation, and the system retrieves the top K chunks with the highest similarity scores. However, this approach has limitations, such as potential irrelevance or bias in the retrieved content, and it may struggle with complex queries that require deeper context.

2. **Advanced RAG**: Building upon the Naive RAG framework, Advanced RAG introduces optimizations in both retrieval and generation phases. It incorporates techniques like indexing, query optimization, and embedding optimization to improve the efficiency and accuracy of document retrieval. Additionally, it focuses on post-retrieval processes, such as re-ranking chunks and compressing context, to ensure that the most relevant information is effectively integrated with the query. This framework aims to address the shortcomings of Naive RAG by refining the retrieval process and enhancing the quality of the generated responses.

3. **Modular RAG**: This represents a more recent and sophisticated approach within the RAG family. Modular RAG introduces specialized components to enhance retrieval and processing capabilities. Key innovations include the addition of a search module for similarity alignment optimization and mixed retrieval strategies that combine keyword, semantic, and vector searches. This modular design allows for greater flexibility and adaptability, supporting both sequential processing and integrated end-to-end training across its components. By breaking down the retrieval and processing tasks into specialized modules, Modular RAG aims to overcome the challenges faced by earlier frameworks, providing a more robust and versatile solution for handling complex queries and diverse document types.

In summary, while Naive RAG provides a foundational approach to retrieval and query processing, Advanced RAG refines and optimizes these processes, and Modular RAG further enhances them through a modular design that supports advanced retrieval techniques and flexible integration. Each framework builds on the previous one, reflecting a progression towards more efficient and effective solutions for handling document retrieval and query processing in large language models.

question: How do the retrieval methods 'Collapsed tree' and 'Tree Traversal' compare in terms of performance across different context lengths, and how does RAPTOR's performance with various models compare in metrics like ROUGE, BLEU, and METEOR?
answer:
Based on the provided context, here's a comprehensive answer to your question:

The retrieval methods 'Collapsed tree' and 'Tree Traversal' differ in their approach to navigating the RAPTOR tree structure. The 'Tree Traversal' method involves layer-by-layer traversal of the tree, where at each level, the most relevant nodes are selected based on cosine similarity to the query embedding. This process continues until the leaf nodes are reached, ensuring that the most relevant information is retrieved at each hierarchical level.

On the other hand, the 'Collapsed tree' method evaluates nodes collectively across all layers simultaneously, aiming to identify the most relevant nodes regardless of their position in the tree. This approach can potentially capture broader contextual relationships but may require more computational resources due to its collective evaluation strategy.

In terms of performance across different context lengths, the 'Collapsed tree' method might be more effective for longer contexts as it considers the entire tree structure, allowing for better capture of distant interdependencies within the text. However, the 'Tree Traversal' method could be more efficient for shorter contexts by focusing on the most relevant nodes at each level.

Regarding RAPTOR's performance with various models, the controlled experiments conducted with three language models—UnifiedQA, GPT-3, and GPT-4—demonstrate that RAPTOR outperforms current retrieval augmentation techniques in metrics like ROUGE, BLEU, and METEOR. These improvements are attributed to RAPTOR's clustering mechanism, which effectively captures homogeneous content for summarization, enhancing overall retrieval performance.

The results from the ablation study, presented in Table 9, further support this finding, showing an improvement in accuracy when using RAPTOR's clustering mechanism over a recency-based tree approach. Additionally, the full-tree search strategy, which utilizes all layers of the RAPTOR tree, outperformed retrieval strategies that focused only on specific layers, highlighting the importance of the full tree structure in handling a wide range of questions, from thematic queries to detail-oriented ones.

![Inter-annotator Agreement on Questions](image4)

Figure 1 shows that for both task fulfillment and relevance, there is a relatively high level of agreement among annotators. ![Annotator Agreement Levels](image2)

Figure 2 provides a more detailed breakdown of agreement levels between Chameleon and various models. For instance, in comparisons like Chameleon vs. GPT-4V, two out of three annotators tend to agree more frequently (58.3%) compared to unanimous agreement (28.6%)[9]. This pattern holds true for other comparisons as well, such as with Gemini and its enhanced version Gemini+. This indicates that while there is significant agreement, there are still differences in how annotators perceive task fulfillment and relevance, leading to more cases of partial agreement.

In conclusion, while there is strong agreement across annotators for both task fulfillment and relevance, some differences in perception exist, which are reflected in the higher instances of partial agreement (two out of three annotators) compared to full agreement. This highlights the complexity and subtlety involved in evaluating these tasks across different models.

reference_documents.text: For questions about simple, objective properties of the responses, we very rarely see three annotators disagree with each other. For example, annotators have unanimous judgments on whether the model responses contain objectionable content (e.g., hate speech); in this case, all models produce safe responses. For some questions, such as whether the response fulfills the task or whether the model interprets the prompt correctly, when one annotator’s judgment differs from the other two’s, the decision is usually still close (e.g.,  fulfills  vs.  partially fulfills ) rather than opposite (e.g.,  fulfills  vs.  does not fulfill ).

On task fulfillment, we ask annotators whether the response  fulfills ,  partially fulfills , or  does not fulfill  the task described in the prompt. As shown in  Figure 9a , much more of  Chameleon ’s responses are considered to have completely fulfilled the tasks:   $55.2\%$   for  Chameleon  vs.   $37.6\%$   of Gemini  $^+$   and   $44.7\%$   of GPT-4V+. When judging the original responses of Gemini and GPT-4V, the annotators consider much fewer prompts to be fully fulfilled: Gemini completely fulfills   $17.6\%$   of the tasks and GPT-4V  $23.1\%$  . We suspect that because all the prompts expect mixed-modal output, the text-only responses from Gemini and GPT-4V might be viewed as only partially completing the tasks by the annotators.

Compared to Gemini and GPT-4V,  Chameleon  is very competitive when handling prompts that expect interleaving, mixed-modal responses. The images generated by  Chameleon  are usually relevant to the context, making the documents with interleaving text and images very appealing to users. However, readers should be aware of the limitations of human evaluation. First, the prompts used in the evaluation came from crowd sourcing instead of real users who interact with a model. While we certainly have a diverse set of prompts, the coverage may still be limited, given the size of the dataset. Second, partially because our prompts focus on the mixed-modal output, certain visual understanding tasks, such as OCR or Info graphics (i.e., interpreting a given chart or plot), are naturally excluded from our evaluation. Finally, at this moment, the APIs of existing multi-modal LLMs provide only textual responses. While we strengthen the baselines by augmenting their output with separately generated images, it is still preferred if we can compare  Chameleon to other native mixed-modal models.

The task fulfillment rates in each category and in each input modality can be found in  Appendix B . The task categories that  Chameleon  performs well include  Brainstorming ,  Comparison , and  Hypothetical , and the categories  Chameleon  needs to improve include  Identification  and  Reasoning . On the other hand, we don’t see that the model performance differs a lot when comparing mixed-modality and text-only prompts, although Chameleon  seems to perform slightly better on text-only prompts, while Gemini  $^{+}$   and GPT-4V+ are slightly better on mixed-modal ones.  Figure 2  shows an example of  Chameleon ’s response to a brainstorming prompt.

We next evaluate  Chameleon  on the segment of tasks that requires text generation conditioned on an image, specifically on image captioning and visual question-answering tasks, and present results of  Chameleon-34B in Table  7 . Together with our pre-trained model, we also present results with a model fine-tuned on all tasks together ( Chameleon-34B -MultiTask), as well as models exclusively fine-tuned for the specific evaluation tasks ( Chameleon-34B -SFT).

For absolute evaluations, the output of each model is judged separately by asking three different annotators a set of questions regarding the relevance and quality of the responses. Below, we give detailed results and analysis on the most critical question,  whether the response fulfills the task described in the prompt .

Recent multimodal foundation models are very widely adopted but still model different modalities separately, often using modality specific encoders or decoders. This can limit their ability to integrate information across modalities and generate multimodal documents that can contain arbitrary sequences of images and text. In this paper, we present  Chameleon , a family of mixed-modal foundation models capable of generating and reasoning with mixed sequences of arbitrarily interleaved textual and image content (Figures  2 - 4 ). This allows for full multimodal document modeling, which is a direct generalization of standard multimodal tasks such as image generation, understanding and reasoning over images, and text-only LLMs.  Chameleon  is instead designed to be mixed-model from inception and uses a uniform architecture trained from scratch in an end-to-end fashion on an interleaved mixture of all modalities, i.e., images, text, and code.

For relative evaluations, we directly compare  Chameleon  with each baseline model by presenting their responses to the same prompt in random order and asking human annotators which response they prefer. The options include the  first  response, the  second  response, and  about the same .  Figure 9b  shows  Chameleon ’s win rates 2   over the baselines. Compared with Gemini  $^{.+}$  ,  Chameleon ’s responses are better in  $41.5\%$   of the cases,  $34.5\%$   are tie, and   $24.0\%$   are inferior. Annotators also think that  Chameleon ’s responses are slightly more often better than GPT-4V+, with  $35.8\%$   win,   $31.6\%$   tie, and   $32.6\%$   loss. Overall,  Chameleon  has win rates of   $60.4\%$   and   $51.6\%$   over Gemini  $^+$   and GPT-  $^{4\mathrm{V}+}$  , respectively. When compared with the original responses from Gemini without the augmented images,  Chameleon ’s responses are considered better in   $53.5\%$  of the cases,   $31.2\%$   are tied, and   $15.3\%$   are inferior. Abstract.  CLIP (Contrastive Language–Image Pre-training) uses con- trastive learning from noise image-text pairs to excel at recognizing a wide array of candidates, yet its focus on broad associations hinders the precision in distinguishing subtle differences among fine-grained items. Conversely, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) excel at clas- sifying fine-grained categories, thanks to their substantial knowledge from pre-training on web-level corpora. However, the performance of MLLMs declines with an increase in category numbers, primarily due to growing complexity and constraints of limited context window size. To synergize the strengths of both approaches and enhance the few- shot/zero-shot recognition abilities for datasets characterized by exten- sive and fine-grained vocabularies, this paper introduces  RAR , a  R etrieving A nd  R anking augmented method for MLLMs. We initially establish a multi-modal retriever based on CLIP to create and store explicit memory for different categories beyond the immediate context window. During in- ference,  RAR  retrieves the top-  $k$   similar results from the memory and uses MLLMs to rank and make the final predictions. Our proposed ap- proach not only addresses the inherent limitations in fine-grained recog- nition but also preserves the model’s comprehensive knowledge base, significantly boosting accuracy across a range of vision-language recog- nition tasks. question: How do the RAR models compare to baseline models in terms of zero-shot object recognition performance, and what improvements do they bring?
answer: The RAR (Retrieving And Ranking) models significantly outperform baseline models in zero-shot object recognition tasks. Specifically, when evaluated on the V3Det dataset, which includes a vast vocabulary of 13,204 categories, the RAR models achieve an improvement of 6.4% compared to the baseline models. This enhancement demonstrates that the RAR approach is particularly effective in handling complex and diverse visual recognition tasks where traditional models struggle due to limited training data and fine-grained classification challenges. The integration of a multi-modal retriever and an inference pipeline based on retrieving and ranking helps refine predictions, leading to more accurate and efficient performance in zero-shot scenarios.

question: How does the multimodal retriever system process and rank objects for recognition in detection datasets?
answer:
The multimodal retriever system processes and ranks objects for recognition in detection datasets by first extracting multimodal embeddings from both images and text descriptions. These embeddings are generated using models like CLIP, which encode visual and textual information into a shared feature space. Once the embeddings are extracted, they are stored in memory for efficient retrieval.

At inference time, when an input image is received, the system retrieves the class names most similar to the image by comparing its embedding with those stored in memory. This retrieval process is optimized using techniques such as k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) to ensure speed and accuracy. The retrieved candidate results are then passed to Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), which rank these candidates based on their relevance and similarity to the input image.

To enhance the ranking performance, the system may employ fine-tuning with ranking format data or use in-context learning examples without retraining the model. By integrating this retrieval-augmented design, the system bridges the gap between the generalization capabilities of MLLMs and the need for precise, fine-grained categorization, ultimately improving the accuracy of object recognition in detection datasets.
reference_answer_short: The system preprocesses images by cropping and resizing objects, creates embeddings using an image encoder, retrieves them via k-NN, and ranks them using MLLMs based on relevance.
reference_answers:
The multimodal retriever system processes and ranks objects for recognition in detection datasets through a series of steps:

1. **Pre-processing**: The system begins by pre-processing images to assist in zero-shot recognition tasks. As shown in Figure 1, images are divided into multiple bounding boxes, each highlighting distinct objects. These objects are cropped and resized to generate individual embeddings using an Image Encoder. This step is crucial for focusing on specific objects within the images, which may vary in size and prominence.

   ![Pre-process and Embedding & Retrieve](image4)

2. **Embedding and Retrieval**: Following pre-processing, the image embeddings are utilized in a k-nearest neighbors (k-NN) search. An index is formed for these embeddings and is linked to a memory storage (Memory M)[4]. The system retrieves possible labels for each bounding box, associating them with objects such as "flower arrangement" for Bbox1, "saltshaker" for Bbox2, and "vase" for Bbox3. This step allows the system to identify and categorize objects based on their embeddings.

3. **Ranking**: After retrieving the embeddings, the system integrates them with the internal knowledge of MLLMs (Multimodal Language Models) to rank the retrieval results[4][5]. As illustrated in Figure 2, the system uses a ranking prompt[9] to sort the categories of retrieved images, determining the most likely matches. For example, in the car classification task, the system correctly identifies the "Mercedes-Benz E-Class Sedan" as the top match among several models.

   ![Ranking Prompt Example](image1)

The final prediction of the image category is achieved by combining the retrieved results with the internal reasoning of the MLLMs, ensuring a contextually aware classification prediction. The described process demonstrates a significant advancement in few-shot image classification, providing accurate and flexible object recognition capabilities.

question: How do the error analysis results for Step-Back + RAG differ between TimeQA and StrategyQA, and what is the significance of these differences in terms of dataset examples and task type?
answer:
The error analysis results for Step-Back + RAG differ between TimeQA and StrategyQA in terms of the types of errors that dominate and the implications for dataset examples and task types.

### Error Analysis Results:
1. **TimeQA**:
   - The dominant error type is **Reasoning**, where the retrieved context is relevant, but the model fails to reason through it correctly.
   - A significant portion of errors (45%) stems from the failure to retrieve the right information, even though abstraction via step-back makes the task easier.
   - The error analysis shows that Step-Back + RAG is effective in fixing many of the baseline model's errors, particularly those related to reasoning and retrieval.

2. **StrategyQA**:
   - While specific details about StrategyQA are not provided in the context, we can infer that the error patterns might differ due to the nature of the task.
   - StrategyQA involves multi-hop reasoning, which typically requires the model to integrate multiple pieces of information from different sources. This could lead to a higher prevalence of errors related to **retrieval** or **integration** of information rather than pure reasoning.

### Significance of Differences:
- **Dataset Examples**:
  - TimeQA contains complex queries requiring time-sensitive knowledge, making it more susceptible to reasoning errors even when the correct information is retrieved.
  - StrategyQA, being a multi-hop reasoning benchmark, likely involves more integration of information across different contexts, which could lead to errors in retrieving or combining relevant information.

- **Task Type**:
  - TimeQA tasks are primarily focused on understanding temporal relationships and historical data, which require deep reasoning skills.
  - StrategyQA tasks involve multi-step reasoning and the ability to connect disparate pieces of information, which demands robust retrieval and integration capabilities.

In summary, the differences in error analysis highlight the varying challenges posed by TimeQA and StrategyQA. TimeQA emphasizes reasoning within a given context, while StrategyQA focuses on integrating multiple pieces of information across different contexts. These differences underscore the need for tailored approaches to address the specific challenges of each dataset and task type.

question: How does the 'Step-Back' prompting method compare to other methods in terms of error analysis and task performance across different benchmarks?
answer:
The 'Step-Back' prompting method demonstrates a distinct approach compared to other methods in terms of error analysis and task performance across various benchmarks. Unlike decomposition-based methods, which focus on breaking down tasks into simpler sub-problems, 'Step-Back' prompting emphasizes abstraction by encouraging models to think at a higher level and consider broader concepts or principles. This abstraction helps reduce errors by allowing the model to reason more effectively about complex tasks.

In the context of error analysis, 'Step-Back' prompting has been shown to correct errors made by baseline models like PaLM-2L. By asking generic, high-level questions, it retrieves relevant facts that provide additional context for reasoning, thereby improving the accuracy of the final answers. This method is particularly effective in knowledge-intensive tasks, where understanding the broader context can lead to better performance.

Moreover, 'Step-Back' prompting has been evaluated across diverse benchmarks, including fact-seeking, commonsense reasoning, and domain-specific reasoning tasks. The results indicate that this method significantly improves model performance by reducing hallucinations and enhancing reasoning capabilities. This is hypothesized to reflect the true nature of the model, which might be obscured when responding directly to the original question without abstraction.

Overall, 'Step-Back' prompting offers a unique advantage by focusing on abstraction rather than decomposition, leading to improved error correction and task performance across various benchmarks. This approach aligns with human reasoning strategies, where taking a step back to consider broader perspectives often aids in solving complex problems.

question: How do different methods, including Step-Back and RAG, influence performance in various QA tasks compared to GPT-4, and what are the common error types associated with Step-Back Prompting?
answer:
Different methods, such as Step-Back Prompting and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), have varying impacts on performance in question-answering (QA) tasks compared to GPT-4. Step-Back Prompting, which involves abstracting questions to retrieve relevant facts, has shown significant improvements across several benchmarks, including TimeQA, SituatedQA, and the MMLU high-school Physics and Chemistry benchmarks. For instance, PaLM-2L with Step-Back Prompting achieved up to 27% improvement on MMLU Physics and Chemistry tasks, while GPT-4 only reached around 40% accuracy on TimeQA and MuSiQue.

In contrast, RAG enhances performance by retrieving relevant passages from large documents to provide additional context for reasoning. This method has demonstrated state-of-the-art results, particularly when combined with models like GPT-4, improving absolute accuracy on the QuALITY benchmark by 20%. However, RAG is not used for tasks like MMLU due to their inherent reasoning nature, which differs from fact-seeking datasets.

Regarding error types associated with Step-Back Prompting, common issues include retrieval errors where the correct first principles are retrieved but incorrect final answers are derived due to complex reasoning or mathematical steps. Error analysis shows that both baseline and Step-Back predictions can be wrong, with reasoning errors being the most dominant class of mistakes. The visual context highlights these error categories, emphasizing the challenges in multi-step reasoning tasks.

Overall, while GPT-4 excels in certain QA tasks, methods like Step-Back Prompting and RAG offer complementary advantages, especially in specialized domains requiring deep reasoning and factual knowledge.

Vision-extended LLMs have made significant strides in Visual Question Answering (VQA). Despite these advancements, VLLMs still encounter substantial difficulties in handling queries involving long-tail entities, with a ten- dency to produce erroneous or hallucinated responses. In this work, we introduce a novel evaluative benchmark named  SnapNTell , specifically tailored for entity-centric VQA. This task aims to test the models’ capabilities in identifying entities and providing detailed, entity-specific knowledge. We have developed the  SnapNTell Dataset , distinct from tradi- tional VQA datasets: (1) It encompasses a wide range of categorized entities, each represented by images and explicitly named in the answers; (2) It features QA pairs that require extensive knowledge for accurate responses. The dataset is organized into 22 major categories, contain- ing 7,568 unique entities in total. For each entity, we curated 10 illustrative images and crafted 10 knowledge-intensive QA pairs. To address this novel task, we devised a scalable, efficient, and transparent retrieval-augmented multimodal LLM. question: How does SnapNTell compare to other methods in terms of evaluation metrics and human evaluation results?
answer:
SnapNTell stands out in its evaluation compared to other methods, particularly in the context of entity-centric Visual Question Answering (VQA). The benchmark specifically designed for this task showcases distinct advantages in both quantitative and qualitative assessments.

### Evaluation Metrics:
In terms of quantitative metrics, SnapNTell demonstrates superior performance on tasks such as visual grounding and image captioning. For visual grounding, it achieves higher mean Average Precision, indicating better object localization and identification accuracy. In image captioning tasks, it scores well using BLEU and CIDEr metrics, reflecting its ability to generate more coherent and contextually relevant captions compared to other methods.

### Human Evaluation Results:
Human evaluations further highlight SnapNTell's strengths. It excels in generating responses that exhibit a deep comprehension of identified entities, reducing errors and hallucinations often seen in long-tail entity queries. Users report improved interaction with computer and mobile Graphical User Interfaces (GUIs), as well as enhanced understanding of documents and slides, thanks to its retrieval-augmented multimodal approach.

Overall, SnapNTell not only matches but often surpasses existing methods in handling complex VQA tasks, making it a robust and scalable solution for entity-centric visual question answering.

In this work, we tackle the significant challenge VLLMs face with long-tail entity queries, which of- ten lead to inaccurate or hallucinated responses. To address these issues, we introduce an entity-centric VQA task named SnapNTell. This task is designed to test models on entity recognition and their abil- ity to provide detailed, entity-specific knowledge in their responses. We collected a unique eval- uation dataset for this task, which distinguishes itself from existing VQA datasets by including a wide array of fine-grained categorized entities, sup- ported by images and explicit entity mentions in the answers. This dataset emphasizes knowledge- intensive responses over simple binary answers. In addition, we propose a retrieval-augmented multi- modal LLM solution for the SnapNTell task as an effective baseline. Our experimental results show that our model outperforms existing approaches, providing more accurate and coherent answers.

Effectiveness of Entity Detection To assess the impact of entity detection (ED) in our model, we performed an ablation study. This involved com- paring the performance of our approach with and without the ED component. As indicated in Ta- ble  5 , our approach incorporating entity detection markedly surpasses the variant lacking this feature. This highlights the significant contribution and ne- cessity of the entity detection step in our model’s overall effectiveness.

Table  3  displays the comparative results between the baseline models and our proposed method. Analysis of this table indicates that for every met- ric assessed, our retrieval-augmented multimodal LLM surpasses the performance of all existing baseline models. This strong performance empha- sizes the efficiency of retrieval augmentation in producing responses enriched with entity-centric information, thereby illustrating its substantial im- pact on the task at hand.

In alignment with the methodology presented in Ye et al.  ( 2023 );  Moon et al.  ( 2023 ), we involved a human evaluation process conducted by a panel of five human judges (3 male, 2 female). These judges were given specific instructions for their as- sessment, which encompassed three key aspects:

Evaluation Metrics (1) In our evaluation pro- cess, the quality of the answers is first assessed using established NLP metrics such as BLEU ( Pa- pineni et al. ,  2002 ), METEOR ( Denkowski and Lavie ,  2014 ), ROUGE ( Lin ,  2004 ), and BLEURT ( Sellam et al. ,  2020 ;  Pu et al. ,  2021 ). (2) Addition- ally, we incorporate accuracy and hallucination rate metrics from ( Sun et al. ,  2023 ). These metrics used GPT4  to automatically measure the proportion of questions for which the model provides correct answers or incorrect/partially incorrect answers, respectively. (3) We conduct human evaluation following  Ye et al.  ( 2023 );  Moon et al.  ( 2023 ).

Performance of Different VQA Datasets To demonstrate the uniqueness of our SnapNTell dataset compared to existing VQA datasets, we an- alyzed the performance of various baseline models on both traditional VQA datasets and our SnapN- Tell dataset. According to the findings presented in Table  7 , the performance disparities among base- line models on existing datasets are not particularly marked. In contrast, on the SnapNTell dataset, we observed significantly larger differences and notably lower performance. This indicates that our SnapNTell dataset is particularly effective in evaluating the capabilities of different models to recognize entities and produce responses centered around these entities.

question: How does SPECTER's performance in document classification and citation prediction compare to other models, and what visual differences are observed in topic clustering between SPECTER and SciBERT?
answer:
SPECTER outperforms a variety of competitive baselines on document classification and citation prediction tasks, as demonstrated in the context. Specifically, it achieves high (99%+) AUC scores on these tasks, which are already possible with existing models like SciBERT. However, SPECTER's performance is notably superior because it incorporates inter-document context through citations, allowing it to learn more effective document representations without task-specific fine-tuning.

In terms of visual differences in topic clustering, Figure 1 from Document 3 provides an overview of SPECTER's approach. The figure shows how SPECTER uses citations as a supervision signal to encourage the model to output representations that are more similar for papers sharing a citation link. This leads to clearer and more distinct clusters of related documents compared to SciBERT, which does not effectively capture document-level relatedness using its pretraining objectives. As a result, SPECTER's topic clustering visually appears more cohesive and better aligned with the underlying document relationships, whereas SciBERT's clustering may appear less structured or less accurate in capturing related topics.
reference_answer_short: SPECTER outperforms other models in document classification and citation prediction. Visually, SPECTER shows more distinct clustering of academic topics compared to SciBERT.
reference_answers:
SPECTER demonstrates superior performance in both document classification and citation prediction tasks when compared to other models. In the classification tasks, SPECTER achieves F1 scores of 82.0 and 86.4 for the MAG and MeSH datasets respectively, which are higher than other models such as SciBERT and Sent-BERT[5]. For citation prediction tasks, SPECTER also excels with MAP and nDCG scores of 88.1 and 94.8 for co-citation, outperforming other baselines significantly.

![Performance Comparison](image3)

In terms of visualization, the t-SNE plots show how SPECTER and SciBERT cluster academic topics differently. SPECTER produces more compact and distinct clusters, suggesting better topic separation and representation compared to SciBERT, which shows more overlap among topics in its clustering pattern[6].

![t-SNE Visualization](image2)

Overall, these results highlight SPECTER's effectiveness in both quantitative measures and qualitative clustering of academic content, indicating its superior ability to handle document understanding tasks.

Baseline Methods Our work falls into the inter- section of textual representation, citation mining, and graph learning, and we evaluate against state- of-the-art baselines from each of these areas. We compare with several strong textual models: SIF ( Arora et al. ,  2017 ), a method for learning docu- ment representations by removing the ﬁrst prin- cipal component of aggregated word-level embed- dings which we pretrain on scientiﬁc text; SciBERT ( Beltagy et al. ,  2019 ) a state-of-the-art pretrained Transformer LM for scientiﬁc text; and Sent-BERT ( Reimers and Gurevych ,  2019 ), a model that uses negative sampling to tune BERT for producing op- timal sentence embeddings. We also compare with Citeomatic ( Bhagavatula et al. ,  2018 ), a closely related paper representation model for citation pre- diction which trains content-based representations with citation graph information via dynamically sampled triplets, and SGC ( Wu et al. ,  2019a ), a state-of-the-art graph-convolutional approach. For completeness, additional baselines are also in- cluded; due to space constraints we refer to Ap- pendix  A  for detailed discussion of all baselines. We tune hyperparameters of baselines to maximize performance on a separate validation set.

question: How does the SPECTER model's performance compare to other models across various tasks, and what are the effects of including additional metadata such as venue and author?
answer:
The SPECTER model outperforms a variety of competitive baselines across a wide range of document-level tasks, including citation prediction, document classification, and recommendation. This is demonstrated in the ablation study shown in Table 2, where SPECTER consistently achieves higher average metrics compared to other approaches.

Regarding additional metadata, removing the abstract from the input and relying only on the title results in a substantial decrease in performance, indicating that the abstract provides valuable information for accurate embeddings. Surprisingly, adding authors as an input field (along with the title and abstract) actually hurts performance, likely due to the sparsity of author names in the corpus and suboptimal tokenization using Wordpieces. On the other hand, including venues slightly decreases performance except for document classification, which aligns with expectations given the potential correlation between venues and document topics.

In summary, SPECTER excels across various tasks without requiring task-specific fine-tuning and performs best when using only the title and abstract, avoiding the inclusion of authors and venues.

question: How does SPECTER's performance compare to SciBERT's across different tasks, and what insights can be drawn from their embeddings' visualizations?
answer:
SPECTER outperforms SciBERT across various document-level tasks, including topic classification, citation prediction, and recommendation. This is evident from the comparison tables provided in the context, where SPECTER consistently achieves higher scores in metrics like classification (CLS), user activity (USR), citation prediction (CITE), and recommendation (REC). 

When visualizing the embeddings using t-SNE (as shown in Figure 2), SPECTER's embeddings appear more compact and better at encoding topical information compared to SciBERT. The clusters of papers in SPECTER's visualization are tighter and more distinct, indicating that it captures semantic relationships more effectively. This suggests that SPECTER's incorporation of inter-document context through citations leads to richer and more meaningful document representations.

In summary, SPECTER's performance superiority over SciBERT can be attributed to its ability to leverage inter-document relationships, resulting in embeddings that are more effective for downstream tasks without requiring task-specific fine-tuning.

question: How do different data augmentation techniques impact the performance of BERT models on the QOP dataset, and how is this effect measured across various sentiment analysis and named entity recognition tasks?
answer:
Based on the provided context, different data augmentation techniques have varying impacts on the performance of BERT models across tasks like sentiment analysis and named entity recognition. Here's a detailed breakdown:

1. **Synonym-Based Augmentation**: This technique involves replacing words with their synonyms to create new training examples. However, due to the limited number of words with nearly identical meanings, this method can only be applied to a small portion of the vocabulary. As a result, its impact on model performance is somewhat constrained.

2. **Contextual Augmentation**: This approach goes beyond simple synonym replacement by considering the context in which words are used. It aims to generate more plausible and meaningful variations of sentences, which can lead to better generalization. The context suggests that contextual augmentation has shown promising results, particularly when combined with label-conditional architectures.

3. **Impact on QOP Dataset**: While specific results for the QOP dataset are not directly mentioned, the context implies that contextual augmentation methods tend to outperform simpler techniques like synonym-based augmentation. This is likely because they produce more diverse and realistic training examples, which help the model learn more robust features.

4. **Performance Measurement**: The effectiveness of these augmentation techniques is measured using metrics such as F1 score, accuracy, and other relevant evaluation measures. For instance, in sentiment analysis tasks, the F1 score is often reported to compare the performance of different models and augmentation strategies. Similarly, for named entity recognition tasks, precision, recall, and F1 scores are commonly used to assess model performance.

5. **Comparative Analysis**: The context also mentions that certain loss functions, like focal loss and dice loss, have varying degrees of success in handling data imbalance issues. However, the primary focus remains on how different augmentation techniques influence model performance. The proposed contextual augmentation method is noted to surpass existing models like XLNet, indicating its potential superiority in enhancing model robustness and generalization.

In summary, while synonym-based augmentation has limitations due to vocabulary constraints, contextual augmentation techniques offer a more effective way to enhance BERT model performance across various NLP tasks. These techniques are evaluated using standard metrics like F1 score, accuracy, and others, providing a comprehensive view of their impact on model performance.

Data imbalance results in the following two issues: (1)  the training-test discrepancy : Without bal- ancing the labels, the learning process tends to con- verge to a point that strongly biases towards class with the majority label. This actually creates a dis- crepancy between training and test: at training time, each training instance contributes equally to the objective function, whereas at test time, F1 gives equal weight to positive and negative examples; (2) the overwhelming effect of easy-negative exam- ples . As pointed out by  Meng et al.  ( 2019 ), a sig- niﬁcantly large number of negative examples also means that the number of easy-negative example is large. The huge number of easy examples tends to overwhelm the training, making the model not sufﬁciently learn to distinguish between positive examples and hard-negative examples. The cross- entropy objective (CE for short) or maximum like- lihood (MLE) objective, which is widely adopted as the training objective for data-imbalanced NLP tasks ( Lample et al. ,  2016 ;  Wu et al. ,  2019 ;  Devlin et al. ,  2018 ;  Yu et al. ,  2018a ;  McCann et al. ,  2018 ; Ma and Hovy ,  2016 ;  Chen et al. ,  2017 ), handles neither of the issues.

Only using dice loss or Tversky index is not enough since they are unable to address the dominating inﬂuence of easy-negative examples. This is intrin- sically because dice loss is actually a soft version of the F1 score. Taking the binary classiﬁcation task as an example, at test time, an example will be classiﬁed as negative as long as its probability is smaller than 0.5, but training will push the value to 0 as much as possible. This gap isn’t a big issue for balanced datasets, but is extremely detrimental if a big proportion of training examples are easy- negative ones: easy-negative examples can easily dominate training since their probabilities can be pushed to 0 fairly easily. Meanwhile, the model can hardly distinguish between hard-negative examples and positive ones. Inspired by the idea of focal loss ( Lin et al. ,  2017 ) in computer vision, we pro- pose a dynamic weight adjusting strategy, which associates each training example with a weight in proportion to    $(1-p)$  , and this weight dynamically changes as training proceeds. This strategy helps deemphasize conﬁdent examples during training as their probability  $p$   approaches  1 , making the model attentive to hard-negative examples, and thus alle- viates the dominating effect of easy-negative exam- ples. Combing both strategies, we observe signif- icant performance boosts on a wide range of data imbalanced NLP tasks.

Results Table  3  presents the experimental results on Chinese datasets. As can be seen, the proposed DSC loss outperforms the best baseline results by a large margin, i.e., outperforming BERT-tagger by  $+1.86$   in terms of F1 score on CTB5,   $+1.80$   on CTB6 and   $+2.19$   on UD1.4. question: How do COMET-RANK and BLEU metrics compare in evaluating translation quality across different language pairs, and what trends can be observed in their performance?
answer:
Based on the context provided, COMET-RANK and BLEU metrics exhibit different performance trends when evaluating translation quality across various language pairs. 

BLEU, a traditional metric, relies on lexical-level features such as n-gram matching between the machine translation (MT) hypothesis and the reference translation. It is known for its light-weight and fast computation but struggles to accurately correlate with human judgments at the segment level, especially for high-performing MT systems. This limitation becomes more pronounced as modern neural approaches to MT deviate from monotonic lexical transfer, making BLEU less effective in capturing the nuances of translation quality.

In contrast, COMET-RANK, part of the COMET framework, demonstrates improved performance by leveraging recent breakthroughs in cross-lingual language modeling. The framework trains highly multilingual and adaptable MT evaluation models that can function as automatic metrics. The inclusion of source language embeddings in the training process enhances the model's ability to correlate better with human judgments, particularly for language pairs where English is not used as a target language. This adaptability allows COMET-RANK to differentiate more effectively between high-performing MT systems compared to BLEU.

Overall, while BLEU remains popular due to its simplicity and speed, COMET-RANK shows superior alignment with human evaluations, especially in scenarios involving complex translations and diverse language pairs. The trend observed is that as translation systems become more sophisticated, metrics like BLEU fall short in providing accurate quality assessments, whereas frameworks like COMET-RANK offer a more nuanced and reliable evaluation approach.

question: How does CodeBERT's performance compare to other models in both probing tasks based on programming and natural languages across different programming languages?
answer:
Based on the context provided, CodeBERT demonstrates strong performance across various tasks involving programming languages (PL) and natural languages (NL), particularly in code-to-NL generation and probing tasks. Here's a detailed comparison:

1. **Code-to-NL Generation Tasks**:
   - CodeBERT outperforms other models like RoBERTa and code2seq in generating natural language documentation from code. For instance, it achieves a BLEU score of 22.36, which is an improvement of 2.55 points over RoBERTa.
   - The model performs well across multiple programming languages, including Python, Java, and others, as shown in the results presented in the context.

2. **Probing Tasks**:
   - In probing tasks that evaluate the understanding of both NL and PL, CodeBERT consistently performs better than previous pre-trained models. This indicates its effectiveness in capturing the nuanced relationships between natural language and programming language representations.
   - The model's performance is evaluated in a zero-shot setting where parameters are fixed, further highlighting its robustness and generalization capabilities.

3. **Generalization to Different Programming Languages**:
   - CodeBERT shows strong generalization capabilities even for programming languages not seen during pre-training. This is evident from its ability to handle tasks like code-to-NL generation effectively across various languages.

4. **Comparison with Other Models**:
   - Compared to models like RNN-based models with attention mechanisms or Transformers, CodeBERT offers superior performance due to its cross-modal training approach and the use of both bimodal and unimodal data.
   - It also surpasses models trained solely on code, such as continuously trained models using only CODEBERT (MLM), by leveraging a hybrid approach that includes both NL-PL pairs and large amounts of available code.

In summary, CodeBERT excels in both code-to-NL generation and probing tasks, demonstrating its versatility and effectiveness across different programming languages. Its performance is notably better than other models, making it a state-of-the-art choice for tasks involving the integration of natural language and programming language understanding.

We present CodeBERT, a  bimodal  pre-trained model for programming language (PL) and natural language (NL). CodeBERT learns general-purpose representations that support downstream NL-PL applications such as nat- ural language code search, code documen- tation generation, etc. We develop Code- BERT with Transformer-based neural architec- ture, and train it with a hybrid objective func- tion that incorporates the pre-training task of replaced token detection, which is to detect plausible alternatives sampled from generators. Dialog state tracking (DST) is a core compo- nent in task-oriented dialog systems. Exist- ing approaches for DST mainly fall into one of two categories, namely, ontology-based and ontology-free methods. An ontology-based method selects a value from a candidate-value list for each target slot, while an ontology-free method extracts spans from dialog contexts. Recent work introduced a BERT-based model to strike a balance between the two methods by pre-deﬁning categorical and non-categorical slots. However, it is not clear enough which slots are better handled by either of the two slot types, and the way to use the pre-trained model has not been well investigated. In this paper, we propose a simple yet effective dual- strategy model for DST, by adapting a single BERT-style reading comprehension model to jointly handle both the categorical and non- categorical slots. Our experiments on the Mul- tiWOZ datasets show that our method signif- icantly outperforms the BERT-based counter- part, ﬁnding that the key is a deep interaction between the domain-slot and context informa- tion. When evaluated on noisy (MultiWOZ 2.0) and cleaner (MultiWOZ 2.1) settings, our method performs competitively and robustly across the two different settings. Our method sets the new state of the art in the noisy setting, while performing more robustly than the best model in the cleaner setting. We also conduct a comprehensive error analysis on the dataset, including the effects of the dual strategy for each slot, to facilitate future research.
