reference_documents.text: In this section, we directly apply our approach to Uyghur, a truly low-resource language with very limited monolingual and parallel resources. We test our model on 199 annotated evaluation documents from the DARPA LORELEI program (the “unsequestered set”) and compare with previ- ously reported results in the cross-lingual setting by  Mayhew et al.  ( 2017 ). Similar to our previous experiments, we transfer from English, use fast- Text embeddings trained on Common Crawl and Wikipedia 6   and a provided dictionary to perform translation, and use GloVe trained on a monolin- gual corpus that has 30 million tokens to perform NER. Results are presented in Table  3 .

Table  1  presents our results on transferring from English to three other languages, alongside results from previous studies. Here “BWET” (bilingual word embedding translation) denotes using the hi- erarchical neural CRF model trained on data trans- lated from English. As can be seen from the ta- ble, our methods outperform previous state-of-the- art results on Spanish and Dutch by a large mar- gin and perform competitively on German even without using any parallel resources. We achieve similar results using different seed dictionaries, and produce the best results when adding the self- attention mechanism to our model.

Another way of performing language indepen- dent transfer resorts to multi-task learning, where a model is trained jointly across different lan- guages by sharing parameters to allow for knowl- edge transfer ( Ammar et al. ,  2016a ;  Yang et al. , 2017 ;  Cotterell and Duh ,  2017 ;  Lin et al. ,  2018 ). However, such approaches usually require some amounts of training data in the target language for bootstrapping, which is different from our un- supervised approach that requires no labeled re- sources in the target language.

Language independent transfer-based ap- proaches build models using language indepen- dent and delexicalized features. For instance, Zirikly and Hagiwara  ( 2015 ) transfers word cluster and gazetteer features through the use of comparable copora.  Tsai et al.  ( 2016 ) links words to Wikipedia entries and uses the entry category as features to train language independent NER models. Recently,  Ni et al.  ( 2017 ) propose to project word embeddings into a common space as language independent features. These approaches utilize such features by training a model on the source language and directly applying it to the target language.

In this section, we study the effects of differ- ent ways of using bilingual word embeddings and the resulting induced translations. As we pointed out previously, ﬁnding translations has two advan- tages: (1) the model can be trained on the exact points from the target embedding space, and (2) the model has access to the target language’s orig- inal character sequences. Here, we conduct abla- tion studies over these two variables. Speciﬁcally, we consider the following three variants.

Bilingual Word Embeddings There have been two general paradigms in obtaining bilingual word vectors besides using dictionaries: through paral- lel corpora and through joint training. Approaches based on parallel corpora usually learn bilingual word embeddings that can produce similar repre- sentations for aligned sentences ( Hermann and Blunsom ,  2014 ;  Chandar et al. ,  2014 ). Jointly- trained models combine the common monolin- gual training objective with a cross-lingual train- ing objective that often comes from parallel corpus ( Zou et al. ,  2013 ;  Gouws et al. ,  2015 ). Recently, unsupervised approaches also have been used to align two sets of word embeddings by learning a mapping through adversarial learning or self- learning ( Zhang et al. ,  2017 ;  Artetxe et al. ,  2017 ; Lample et al. ,  2018 ).

In this paper, we propose two methods to tackle the cross-lingual NER problem under the unsuper- vised transfer setting. To address the challenge of lexical mapping, we ﬁnd translations of words in a shared embedding space built from a seed lex- icon. To alleviate word order divergence across languages, we add a self-attention mechanism to our neural architecture. With these methods com- bined, we are able to achieve state-of-the-art or competitive results on commonly tested languages under a cross-lingual setting, with lower resource requirements than past approaches. We also eval- uate the challenges of applying these methods to an extremely low-resource language, Uyghur.

In our experiments, we start with models trained in English as the source language on the CoNLL 2002 and 2003 datasets and transfer them into Spanish, Dutch, and German as the target lan- guages. Our approach obtains new state-of-the- art cross-lingual results in Spanish and Dutch, and competitive results in German, even without a dictionary, completely removing the need for re- sources such as Wikipedia and parallel corpora. Next, we transfer English using the same approach into Uyghur, a truly low-resource language. With signiﬁcantly fewer cross-lingual resources, our ap- proach can still perform competitively with previ- ous best results.

Annotation projection methods create training data by using parallel corpora to project annota- tions from the source to the target language. Such approaches have been applied to many tasks un- der the cross-lingual setting, such as POS tag- ging ( Yarowsky et al. ,  2001 ;  Das and Petrov ,  2011 ; T¨ ackstr¨ om et al. ,  2013 ;  Fang and Cohn ,  2016 ), mention detection ( Zitouni and Florian ,  2008 ) and parsing ( Hwa et al. ,  2005 ;  McDonald et al. ,  2011 ).

Our method performs competitively, consid- ering that we use a much smaller dictionary than  Mayhew et al.  ( 2017 ) and no knowledge from Wikipedia in Uyghur. Our best results come from a combined approach: using word embeddings to translate words that are not covered by  Mayhew et al.  ( 2017 )’s dictionary (last line of Table  3 ). Note that for the CoNLL languages, Mayhew et al.  ( 2017 ) used Wikipedia for the Wikiﬁer fea- tures ( Tsai et al. ,  2016 ), while for Uyghur they used it for translating named entities, which is cru- cial for low-resource languages when some named entities are not covered by the dictionary or the translation is not reliable. We suspect that the un- reliable translation of named entities is the ma- jor reason why our method alone performs worse but performs better when combined with their data that has access to higher quality translations of named entities.

question: What are the key differences in task completion and performance metrics between the LANI and CHAI datasets based on the comparative analysis of navigation instructions and methods?
answer:
Based on the comparative analysis provided in the context, there are several key differences in task completion and performance metrics between the LANI and CHAI datasets:

1. **Task Complexity**: 
   - LANI is a landmark navigation task where instructions typically involve moving between landmarks. The average instruction contains around 4.7 actions, which are primarily navigation-related.
   - CHAI, on the other hand, combines both navigation and simple manipulation tasks (e.g., picking up objects, opening containers). The average instruction contains approximately 7.7 actions, making it more complex.

2. **Performance Metrics**:
   - Task Completion Accuracy: On LANI, models like CHAPLOT18 and MISRA17 perform reasonably well, with improvements noted in task completion accuracy. However, on CHAI, these models struggle significantly, especially with manipulation tasks.
   - Stop Distance Error: For LANI, the focus is on completing the task within a certain aerial distance from the goal. In contrast, for CHAI, the stop distance error metric becomes crucial as the tasks involve more complex interactions beyond just navigation.

3. **Model Performance**:
   - On LANI, methods such as CHAPLOT18 and MISRA17 show notable improvements in task completion accuracy, with CHAPLOT18 improving by 5%.
   - On CHAI, however, both CHAPLOT18 and MISRA17 fail to learn effectively, particularly in handling manipulation tasks. The proposed model outperforms these baselines in terms of stop distance error.

4. **Dataset Characteristics**:
   - LANI consists of 6,000 sequences of natural language instructions, each containing an average of 4.7 instructions.
   - CHAI has 1,596 instruction sequences, with an average of 7.7 instructions per sequence, indicating a higher level of complexity and interaction.

In summary, while LANI focuses on simpler navigation tasks with fewer actions per instruction, CHAI presents a more challenging environment due to its combination of navigation and manipulation tasks, leading to different performance outcomes and requiring more sophisticated models to handle the increased complexity.

On C HAI , C HAP - LOT 18 and M ISRA 17 both fail to learn, while our approach shows an improvement on stop dis- tance (SD). However, all models perform poorly on C HAI , especially on manipulation (MA).

Evaluation Metrics We evaluate using the met- rics described in Section  6 : stop distance (SD) and task completion (TC) for L ANI , and stop distance (SD) and manipulation accuracy (MA) for C HAI . To evaluate the goal prediction, we report the real distance of the predicted goal from the annotated goal and the percentage of correct predictions. We consider a goal correct if it is within a distance of 5 . 0  for L ANI  and  1 . 0  for C HAI . We also report human evaluation for L ANI  by asking raters if the generated path follows the instruction on a Likert- type scale of 1–5. Raters were shown the gener- ated path, the reference path, and the instruction.

Our data collection is related to existing work. L ANI  is inspired by the HCRC Map Task ( An- derson et al. ,  1991 ), where a leader directs a fol- lower to navigate between landmarks on a map. We use a similar task, but our scalable data collec- tion process allows for a signiﬁcantly larger cor- pus. We also provide an interactive navigation environment, instead of only map diagrams. Un- like Map Task, our leaders and followers do not interact in real time. This abstracts away inter- action challenges, similar to how the SAIL nav- igation corpus was collected ( MacMahon et al. , 2006 ). C HAI  instructions were collected using scenarios given to workers, similar to the ATIS collection process ( Hemphill et al. ,  1990 ;  Dahl et al. ,  1994 ). Recently, multiple 3D research envi- ronments were released. L ANI  has a signiﬁcantly larger state space than existing navigation envi- ronments ( Hermann et al. ,  2017 ;  Chaplot et al. , 2018 ), and C HALET , the environment used for C HAI , is larger and has more complex manipu- lation compared to similar environments ( Gordon et al. ,  2018 ;  Das et al. ,  2018 ). In addition, only synthetic language data has been released for these environment. An exception is the Room-to-Room dataset ( Anderson et al. ,  2018 ) that makes use of an environment of connected panoramas of house settings. Although it provides a realistic vision challenge, unlike our environments, the state space is limited to a small number of panoramas and ma- nipulation is not possible.

We compare our approach to multiple recent methods. Experiments on the L ANI  navigation task indicate that decomposing goal prediction and action generation signiﬁcantly improves in- struction execution performance. While we ob- serve similar trends on the C HAI  instructions, re- sults are overall weaker, illustrating the complex- ity of the task. We also observe that inherent ambiguities in instruction following make exact goal identiﬁcation difﬁcult, as demonstrated by imperfect human performance. However, the gap to human-level performance still remains large across both tasks. Our code and data are available at  github.com/clic-lab/ciff .

We introduce two new benchmark tasks with different levels of complexity of goal prediction and action generation. L ANI  is a 3D navigation environment and corpus, where an agent navigates between landmarks. The corpus includes 6,000 sequences of natural language instructions, each containing on average 4.7 instructions. C HAI  is a corpus of 1,596 instruction sequences, each in- cluding 7.7 instructions on average, for C HALET , a 3D house environment ( Yan et al. ,  2018 ). In- structions combine navigation and simple manipu- lation, including moving objects and opening con- tainers. Both tasks require solving language chal- lenges, including spatial and temporal reasoning, as well as complex perception and planning prob- lems. While L ANI  provides a task where most in- structions include a single goal, the C HAI  instruc- tions often require multiple intermediate goals. For example, the household instruction in Fig- ure  1  can be decomposed to eight goals: opening the cupboard, picking each item and moving it to the cupboard, and closing the cupboard. Achiev- ing each goal requires multiple actions of differ- ent types, including moving and acting on objects. This allows us to experiment with a simple varia- tion of our model to generate intermediate goals.

To isolate navigation performance on C HAI , we limit our train and test data to instructions that in- clude navigation actions only. The S TOP  baseline on these instructions gives a stop distance (SD) of 3.91, higher than the average for the entire data as these instructions require more movement. Our approach gives a stop distance (SD) of 3.24, a   $17\%$  reduction of error, signiﬁcantly better than the   $8\%$  reduction of error over the entire corpus.

question: How does the 'Our Approach' method perform compared to other methods in terms of Stop Distance (SD) and Task Completion (TC) across the LANI and CHAI datasets, and what are the potential factors influencing its performance?
answer:
The 'Our Approach' method demonstrates superior performance compared to other methods in terms of Stop Distance (SD) and Task Completion (TC) across both the LANI and CHAI datasets. Specifically, on the LANI dataset, it achieves a stop distance (SD) of 8.67 and a task completion (TC) accuracy of 35.83, outperforming baselines like STOP, RANDOMWALK, and MOSTFREQUENT. On the CHAI dataset, it shows an SD of 2.12 and a manipulation accuracy (MA) of 40.3, significantly improving upon previous methods such as CHAPLOT18 and MISRA17.

Several factors contribute to its improved performance. First, the approach effectively separates goal prediction from action generation, allowing for more precise and interpretable goal representation. This separation helps reduce ambiguity and improves navigation behavior. Second, the method incorporates intermediate goals, which enhances planning complexity and execution quality. Additionally, the use of a horizon during training encourages learning even after errors, further refining the model's performance.

However, challenges remain, particularly in handling instructions with temporal coordination or co-reference, which can limit the model's ability to resolve references to previous instructions. Despite these limitations, the 'Our Approach' method represents a significant advancement in instruction-following tasks, showing robustness against simple biases and providing a strong foundation for future research in this area.

Evaluation Metrics We evaluate using the met- rics described in Section  6 : stop distance (SD) and task completion (TC) for L ANI , and stop distance (SD) and manipulation accuracy (MA) for C HAI . To evaluate the goal prediction, we report the real distance of the predicted goal from the annotated goal and the percentage of correct predictions. We consider a goal correct if it is within a distance of 5 . 0  for L ANI  and  1 . 0  for C HAI . We also report human evaluation for L ANI  by asking raters if the generated path follows the instruction on a Likert- type scale of 1–5. Raters were shown the gener- ated path, the reference path, and the instruction.

Goal prediction is related to referring expres- sion interpretation ( Matuszek et al. ,  2012a ;  Krish- namurthy and Kollar ,  2013 ;  Kazemzadeh et al. , 2014 ;  Kong et al. ,  2014 ;  Yu et al. ,  2016 ;  Mao et al. , 2016 ;  Kitaev and Klein ,  2017 ). While our model solves a similar problem for goal prediction, we focus on detecting visual goals for actions, includ- ing both navigation and manipulation, as part of an instruction following model. Using formal goal representation for instruction following was stud- ied by  MacGlashan et al.  ( 2015 ). In contrast, our model generates a probability distribution over im- ages, and does not require an ontology.

Our ablations (Table  3 ) demonstrate the impor- tance of each of the components of the model. We ablate the action generation RNN (w/o RNN), completely remove the language input (w/o Lan- guage), and train the model jointly (w/joint Learn- ing). On C HAI  especially, ablations results in models that display ineffective behavior. Of the ablations, we observe the largest beneﬁt from decomposing the learning and using supervised learning for the language problem.

We compare our approach to multiple recent methods. Experiments on the L ANI  navigation task indicate that decomposing goal prediction and action generation signiﬁcantly improves in- struction execution performance. While we ob- serve similar trends on the C HAI  instructions, re- sults are overall weaker, illustrating the complex- ity of the task. We also observe that inherent ambiguities in instruction following make exact goal identiﬁcation difﬁcult, as demonstrated by imperfect human performance. However, the gap to human-level performance still remains large across both tasks. Our code and data are available at  github.com/clic-lab/ciff .

We also evaluate our approach with access to oracle goals (Table  3 ). We observe this im- proves navigation performance signiﬁcantly on both tasks. However, the model completely fails to learn a reasonable manipulation behavior for C HAI . This illustrates the planning complexity of this domain. A large part of the improvement in measured navigation behavior is likely due to eliminating much of the ambiguity the automated metric often fails to capture.

We propose a model for instruction following with explicit separation of goal prediction and action generation. Our representation of goal prediction is easily interpretable, while not requiring the de- sign of logical ontologies and symbolic represen- tations. A potential limitation of our approach is cascading errors. Action generation relies com- pletely on the predicted goal and is not exposed to the language otherwise. This also suggests a second related limitation: the model is unlikely to successfully reason about instructions that in- clude constraints on the execution itself. While the model may reach the ﬁnal goal correctly, it is unlikely to account for the intermediate trajectory constraints. As we show (Table  2 ), such instruc- tions are common in our data. These two limita- tions may be addressed by allowing action genera- tion access to the instruction. Achieving this while retaining an interpretable goal representation that clearly determines the execution is an important direction for future work. Another important open question concerns automated evaluation, which re- mains especially challenging when instructions do not only specify goals, but also constraints on how to achieve them. Our resources provide the plat- form and data to conduct this research.

question: How does the SciIE model perform compared to other models in terms of precision, recall, and F1 score across various NLP tasks, and what additional insights can be drawn from its multitask learning approach?
answer:
The SciIE model demonstrates superior performance compared to other models across various NLP tasks, particularly in scientific information extraction. In terms of precision, recall, and F1 score, the model outperforms previous systems such as E2E Rel and E2E Coref in entity recognition, relation extraction, and coreference resolution tasks. For instance, in entity recognition, SciIE achieves a significant improvement over E2E Rel, with relative improvements of 1.8% and 2.7% when using and not using ELMO, respectively. Similarly, for relation extraction, it shows a 13.1% relative improvement over E2E Rel without ELMO and a 7.4% improvement with ELMO. In coreference resolution, SciIE also surpasses E2E Coref by 4.5% relative improvement.

The multitask learning approach employed by SciIE is a key factor in its success. By sharing span representations across entity, relation, and coreference tasks, the model reduces cascading errors and leverages cross-sentence relations through coreference links. This unified framework allows the model to benefit from additional tasks during training, leading to improved performance in each individual task. The ablation studies further confirm that including multiple tasks in the learning objective enhances performance, with each added task contributing positively to the overall results.

Overall, the SciIE model's ability to integrate and optimize across multiple NLP tasks highlights the effectiveness of multitask learning in scientific knowledge graph construction. Despite these advancements, there remains a noticeable gap between human-level performance and the current machine learning systems, indicating opportunities for further research and development in this area.

question: How does the performance of the SciIE multitask system compare to single-task systems for entity recognition, relation extraction, and coreference resolution, and what benefits are observed with coreference inclusion in precision and recall?
answer:
The SciIE multitask system demonstrates superior performance compared to single-task systems across entity recognition, relation extraction, and coreference resolution. Specifically, for entity recognition, the multitask approach achieves an F1 score of 68.1, which is a significant improvement over the single-task baseline of 65.7 (a 3.4% relative increase). Similarly, for relation extraction, the multitask system scores 39.5, outperforming the single-task baseline of 37.9 (a 4.2% relative improvement). In coreference resolution, the multitask system reaches an F1 score of 58.0, compared to the single-task baseline of 55.3 (a 4.9% relative improvement).

Incorporating coreference resolution into the multitask setup also brings notable benefits in terms of precision and recall. For instance, entity recognition sees a substantial boost when coreference resolution is included, with a 7.1% relative improvement in F1 score. This indicates that leveraging coreference links helps the model better understand overlapping spans and improves overall accuracy.

Overall, the multitask framework not only enhances performance across all three tasks but also reduces cascading errors and leverages cross-sentence relations through coreference links, leading to more robust and accurate scientific knowledge graph construction.

question: How do the performances on the GLUE benchmark differ between BERT models and CNN models, and what can be inferred about their strengths from these comparisons?
answer:
Based on the context provided, there are several key differences in performance between BERT models and CNN models when evaluated on tasks like the GLUE benchmark:

1. **BERT Models Outperform CNNs on Certain Tasks**: 
   - The BERT models (both BASE and LARGE versions) consistently outperform the CNN models across multiple tasks, as seen in Table 3. For instance, the BERTBASE model achieves a test F1 score of 96.4, while the CNN Large + fine-tune model reaches 95.6. This suggests that BERT models are generally more effective at capturing complex language patterns and contextual understanding.

2. **Strengths of BERT Models**:
   - BERT models benefit from pre-training on large-scale datasets using self-supervised learning objectives, which allows them to capture richer semantic representations. This is particularly evident in tasks requiring nuanced understanding of word meanings and sentence structures, such as the Word in Context (WiC) task from the SuperGLUE benchmark.
   - The addition of word-supersense information in SenseBERT further enhances its performance, surpassing even the larger BERTLARGE model in specific tasks. This indicates that incorporating lexical semantics into BERT's architecture can significantly improve its effectiveness.

3. **Strengths of CNN Models**:
   - While CNN models may not match the overall performance of BERT models, they still perform competitively in certain scenarios. For example, on some tasks involving sentence pairs (like MRPC and RTE), STILTs (which uses CNNs) performs better than BERT. This suggests that CNNs might have an edge in tasks where simpler, hierarchical pooling operations are sufficient for capturing relevant features.
   - CNN models also tend to be faster to train compared to BERT models, despite having fewer parameters. This makes them a viable option for applications where computational efficiency is a priority.

4. **Trade-offs Between Models**:
   - BERT models, while more powerful, are larger and require more computational resources for training and inference. This can be a limitation in resource-constrained environments.
   - CNN models, on the other hand, offer a balance between performance and efficiency, making them suitable for tasks where speed and simplicity are more critical than achieving state-of-the-art results.

In summary, BERT models generally excel in tasks requiring deep contextual understanding, while CNN models remain competitive in specific scenarios and offer advantages in terms of computational efficiency. The choice between the two depends on the specific requirements of the task, including the need for accuracy versus computational resources.

The comparative analysis of BERT and CNN models on the GLUE benchmark reveals distinct strengths in language understanding tasks. 

![Figure 1](image2)

**BERT vs. CNN on GLUE Tasks:**
- **BERT Models**: BERT_BASE and BERT_LARGE consistently outperform CNN models such as CNN Base and CNN Large across various GLUE tasks. For example, BERT_LARGE achieves superior results on CoLA (60.5 mcc), QNLI (91.1 acc), and RTE (70.1 acc), as seen in Figure 1. The average performance of BERT_LARGE is 81.9, which is higher compared to CNN Large (78.6).
- **CNN Models**: While CNN models like CNN Base and CNN Large show competitive performance in some tasks (e.g., SST-2 and MRPC), they generally fall behind BERT models. CNN Large has an average score of 78.6, with particular strengths in SST-2 (94.6 acc) and MRPC (83.7 F1).

![Figure 2](image5)

**F1 Score Analysis in Different Contexts:**
- **Development and Test F1 Scores**: Further analysis in Figure 2 demonstrates that CNN Large models combined with ELMo or fine-tuning show improvements, achieving test F1 scores like 93.5 for CNN Large + fine-tune. However, BERT models still present robust performance with BERT_LARGE achieving a test F1 score of 92.8.

![Figure 3](image1)

- **Additional Task Performance**: Figure 3 reinforces the trend with CNN Large + fine-tune achieving the highest F1 scores, yet the consistent high performance of BERT across different datasets and tasks highlights its adaptability and strength in language representation.

**Inferences on Strengths:**
- **BERT's Strength**: The findings suggest that BERT's architecture, possibly due to its transformer-based design, is inherently more suited for capturing complex language patterns, resulting in higher performance across diverse tasks[1].
- **CNN's Use Cases**: CNN models, while less effective in aggregate, show potential when enhanced with additional methods like ELMo or fine-tuning, suggesting their utility in specialized scenarios or when integrated with complementary techniques[10].

Overall, the comparative performance underscores the effectiveness of BERT models in natural language processing tasks, attributed to their robust and flexible architecture.

reference_documents.text: Experiments on the GLUE ( Wang et al. ,  2018 ) benchmark show strong gains over the state of the art for each task, including a 9.1 point gain on RTE over  Radford et al.  ( 2018 ). These improvements are consistent with, if slightly behind, BERT ( De- vlin et al. ,  2018 ), which we will discuss in more detail in the next section. We also show that it is possible to stack task-speciﬁc architectures for NER and constituency parsing on top of our pre- trained representations, and achieve new state-of- the-art performance levels for both tasks. We also present extensive experimental analysis to better understand these results, showing that (1) hav- ing multiple sentences in each training example is crucial for many tasks; (2) pre-training contin- ues to improve performance with up to 18B tokens and would likely continue to improve with more data; and ﬁnally (3) our novel cloze-driven train- ing regime is more effective than predicting left and right tokens separately.

We present a new approach for pretraining a bi-directional transformer model that provides signiﬁcant performance gains across a vari- ety of language understanding problems. Our model solves a cloze-style word reconstruction task, where each word is ablated and must be predicted given the rest of the text. Experi- ments demonstrate large performance gains on GLUE and new state of the art results on NER as well as constituency parsing benchmarks, consistent with BERT. We also present a de- tailed analysis of a number of factors that con- tribute to effective pretraining, including data domain and size, model capacity, and varia- tions on the cloze objective.

question: How does the performance of CNN models differ with and without additional finetuning or stacking architectures on various NLP tasks?
answer:
The performance of CNN models in NLP tasks can vary significantly depending on whether additional finetuning or stacking architectures are employed. When CNN models are used without these enhancements, they often rely on simpler configurations, such as a single convolutional layer combined with pooling operations. This approach can be effective for certain tasks, particularly those involving shorter sentences or sentiment analysis, where the model captures basic semantic patterns efficiently.

However, when additional finetuning or stacking architectures are applied, CNN models can achieve higher accuracy and better capture complex linguistic structures. For instance, stacking multiple convolutional layers allows the model to learn more abstract features from the text sequences, which is beneficial for tasks like document classification or natural language sequence matching. Finetuning the model on specific datasets can also improve its performance by adapting the learned features to the nuances of the particular task.

In some cases, CNN models outperform other architectures like LSTMs when additional enhancements are applied. For example, on the AG News dataset, CNN models can leverage more trainable parameters to achieve higher accuracy compared to SWEM models. However, for tasks that require capturing word-order dependencies, such as sentiment analysis, simpler models like SWEMs can still perform comparably or even better than CNNs without these enhancements.

Overall, the choice between using CNN models with or without additional finetuning or stacking architectures depends on the specific NLP task and the complexity of the data being processed. While simpler configurations may suffice for certain tasks, more complex setups can lead to improved performance on others.

answer:

### Performance Comparison of CNN Large vs. BERT_LARGE

The CNN Large model and BERT_LARGE are both strong performers in various natural language processing (NLP) tasks, but their performance varies depending on the specific task and dataset.

3. **General Observations:**
   - **Task Sensitivity:** Sentiment analysis tasks are more sensitive to word-order features than topic categorization tasks. While CNN Large performs well on sentiment analysis tasks, BERT_LARGE's ability to capture long-range dependencies and contextual information gives it an edge in more complex tasks like NER.
   - **Model Size and Training Efficiency:** BERT_LARGE is significantly larger than CNN Large, with more parameters. This makes BERT_LARGE more powerful but also slower to train. ### Implications of Increasing Training Data Size on Average GLUE Score

The General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark is a collection of diverse NLP tasks designed to evaluate the performance of language understanding models. The average GLUE score is a composite metric that reflects a model's overall performance across these tasks.

1. **Impact of Training Data Size:**
   - **Improved Performance:** Generally, increasing the size of the training data leads to better performance on the GLUE benchmark. Larger datasets allow models to learn more robust representations and generalize better to unseen data.
   - **Diminishing Returns:** There is often a point of diminishing returns where additional data provides minimal improvement in performance. For models like BERT_LARGE, which already have a large number of parameters, the marginal gains from additional data may be smaller compared to smaller models like CNN Large.
   - **Task-Specific Benefits:** Some tasks within the GLUE benchmark may benefit more from increased training data than others. For example, tasks involving complex reasoning or long-range dependencies might see more significant improvements compared to simpler tasks like sentiment analysis.

2. **Implications for Model Selection:**
   - **Resource Allocation:** If computational resources are limited, it may be more beneficial to focus on improving the quality and diversity of the training data rather than simply increasing the size of the dataset for larger models like BERT_LARGE.
   - **Hybrid Approaches:** Combining smaller, more efficient models like CNN Large with carefully curated, high-quality training data can sometimes yield performance comparable to larger models while being more resource-efficient.

In summary, while BERT_LARGE generally outperforms CNN Large in tasks requiring deep contextual understanding, such as NER, CNN Large remains a strong contender for tasks where computational efficiency is crucial. Increasing the size of the training data typically improves the average GLUE score, but the benefits diminish as the dataset grows, and the impact varies depending on the specific tasks within the benchmark.

question: How does the alignment of word embeddings impact BLEU scores in different language translation tasks?
answer:
The alignment of word embeddings has a notable impact on BLEU scores in various language translation tasks, as indicated by the context provided. In bilingual translation tasks, such as Portuguese to English (PT → EN), pre-training and aligning word embeddings can lead to significant improvements in BLEU scores. For instance, Table 4 shows that aligning embeddings results in higher BLEU scores compared to non-aligned models.

In multilingual translation tasks, particularly when translating into English from languages like Galician (GL) or Russian (RU), pre-training and aligning embeddings also enhance performance. Table 5 illustrates this, where pre-trained models achieve higher BLEU scores than those without pre-training. This suggests that aligning embeddings is beneficial for improving translation quality, especially in scenarios involving multiple languages.

Moreover, the effectiveness of embedding alignment varies with the similarity of the languages involved. For example, Slavic languages, which are partially mutually intelligible but have rich morphology, benefit more from aligned embeddings due to the challenges posed by sparsity in trained embeddings.

In summary, aligning word embeddings generally improves BLEU scores, particularly in multilingual settings and for languages with complex morphological structures. However, the extent of improvement depends on the specific language pair and the resources available for training.

question: How does pre-training affect translation accuracy across different language pairs, and what role does training set size and language similarity play in this effect?
answer:
Pre-training of word embeddings has a significant impact on translation accuracy, particularly in low-resource language scenarios. The effectiveness of pre-training varies depending on the size of the training set and the similarity between the languages involved.

In general, pre-trained embeddings are most effective when there is a limited amount of training data available. This is because they provide a richer representation of less frequent words and phrases, which helps the model to better understand and translate these elements. However, as the amount of training data increases, the benefits of pre-training tend to diminish, suggesting that there is a "sweet-spot" where pre-training is most useful.

Language similarity also plays a crucial role. Pre-trained embeddings are more effective for translation pairs that are linguistically closer, such as English-German, compared to more dissimilar pairs like BE/RU (Belarusian-Russian). This indicates that the closer the languages, the more beneficial pre-training can be in improving translation accuracy.

Additionally, while pre-training may not be necessary for bilingual scenarios, it becomes increasingly helpful in multilingual settings. This is because shared encoders or decoders across multiple languages can leverage the additional knowledge provided by pre-trained embeddings, further enhancing translation performance.

Overall, the combination of a smaller training set and higher linguistic similarity tends to maximize the benefits of pre-training in neural machine translation systems.

answer:
The alignment of word embeddings has varying effects on translation performance depending on the language pairs and training scenarios. In bilingual settings, a priori alignment of embeddings may not be necessary, as the neural machine translation (NMT) system can learn reasonable projections during training. However, in multilingual systems, aligning embeddings can be beneficial, especially when dealing with low-resource languages.

Regarding the F-measure scores for target words based on their frequency in the training corpus, the data suggests that there is a sweet spot where word embeddings are most effective—this occurs when there is very little training data but not so little that the system cannot be trained at all. The F-measure tends to increase as the frequency of target words in the training corpus increases, indicating better performance for more frequently occurring words. This trend is illustrated in Figure 2, which shows the F-measure of target words across different frequency ranges in the training corpus. 

In summary, while embedding alignment can enhance performance in multilingual scenarios, its necessity in bilingual contexts is less clear. Additionally, the effectiveness of word embeddings improves with higher frequency of target words in the training data, as reflected by the increasing F-measure scores.

question: How does the removal of specific components like R-GCN, relation types, and specific relation types (e.g., MATCH, COREF) impact the performance of models under unmasked and masked conditions?
answer:
The removal of specific components such as the R-GCN module, relation types, and individual relation types (e.g., MATCH, COREF) generally leads to a decline in model performance under both unmasked and masked conditions. This is evident from the experiments described in the context, where models without these components or with ablated relations perform worse compared to those that include them.

Under unmasked conditions, the absence of R-GCN results in a noticeable drop in performance, suggesting that the model struggles to learn dependencies on its own without this component. Similarly, removing specific relation types like MATCH or COREF also negatively impacts performance, indicating their importance in capturing relevant connections between entities.

In the masked setting, the impact is somewhat less pronounced, but still observable. The model's ability to handle coreferential mentions is affected when certain components are removed, leading to a decrease in effectiveness. question: How does the inclusion of coreference information impact the performance of Entity-GCN models in unmasked and masked settings?
answer:
The inclusion of coreference information significantly enhances the performance of Entity-GCN models, particularly in unmasked settings. In these scenarios, the model benefits from a richer contextual understanding, as it can leverage shared span representations refined by incorporating textualized information from relations and coreferences. This broader context allows the model to better capture the relationships between entities, leading to improved accuracy in entity recognition and relation extraction tasks.

In contrast, in masked settings, where all mentions are treated as 'unknown' tokens, the impact of coreference information is less pronounced. The model's reliance on GloVe embeddings means that predictions are equivalent to random guesses, as it lacks the contextual clues provided by the surrounding text. However, even in this setting, the incorporation of coreference information can still offer some advantages, albeit to a lesser extent.

Overall, the effectiveness of coreference information varies depending on the complexity of the task and the availability of contextual data. In unmasked settings, where the model has access to more detailed textual information, the integration of coreference data leads to substantial improvements in performance. In masked settings, while the benefits are reduced, they still contribute positively to the model's ability to reason about entities and their relationships.
reference_answer_short: Inclusion of coreference information in Entity-GCN models improves performance in masked settings but has a marginal effect in unmasked settings.
reference_answers:
The inclusion of coreference information in Entity-GCN models has different impacts depending on whether the dataset is unmasked or masked.

![Performance of different models](image4)

In the unmasked setting, the Entity-GCN model without coreference achieves a test accuracy of 67.6% and a development accuracy of 64.8%. When coreference information is included, the test accuracy slightly decreases to 66.4%, but the development accuracy increases to 65.3%. This suggests that while coreference information might not significantly enhance the overall performance in unmasked settings, it can contribute to the robustness of the model during development.

In contrast, for the masked setting, the inclusion of coreference information is more beneficial. The Entity-GCN model without coreference scores 70.5% on the masked development set, whereas the ensemble model with coreference achieves 71.6%. This indicates that coreference information plays a crucial role in improving the model's ability to handle masked data, likely because it helps the model make connections between entities that are otherwise obscured by masking[10].

![Model configurations and performance](image2)

Thus, coreference information is particularly useful in contexts where the model needs to infer connections between entities without relying on explicit context clues, such as in masked datasets[2]. This highlights the importance of leveraging coreference information to enhance model performance in scenarios where relational data might be incomplete or hidden.

question: How does the DyGIE system perform on entity and relation extraction tasks across different datasets, and what are the effects of using coreference and relation propagation layers on these tasks?
answer:
The DyGIE system demonstrates significant improvements in both entity recognition and relation extraction tasks across various datasets and domains. It achieves these enhancements by leveraging a unified framework that integrates multiple information extraction tasks, such as entity recognition, relation extraction, and coreference resolution, through shared span representations.

One of the key features of DyGIE is its ability to handle overlapping spans, which is crucial for accurately identifying nested entities. This capability leads to substantial F1 score improvements on entity recognition tasks, particularly in scenarios where entities may overlap or be nested within each other.

Additionally, the use of coreference propagation layers plays a vital role in enhancing the quality of extracted information. By propagating coreference links, DyGIE can better understand the relationships between different mentions of the same entity across sentences, leading to more accurate and coherent knowledge graphs. This approach helps reduce cascading errors that often occur when tasks are processed sequentially without considering their interdependencies.

Furthermore, the incorporation of relation propagation layers allows DyGIE to leverage cross-sentence relations effectively. This is particularly beneficial in scientific literature, where relationships between entities may span multiple sentences. By integrating these layers, DyGIE can capture more comprehensive and contextually rich relations, thereby improving the overall performance in relation extraction tasks.

In summary, DyGIE's multi-task learning framework, combined with coreference and relation propagation layers, significantly boosts its performance in entity and relation extraction tasks across diverse datasets. This integrated approach not only enhances accuracy but also ensures more robust and reliable information extraction, especially in complex domains like scientific literature.
reference_answer_short: DyGIE achieves the highest scores across all datasets for both entity and relation extraction tasks. Coreference and relation propagation enhance F1 scores, with the best results seen with certain iterations.
reference_answers:
The DyGIE system demonstrates notable performance in entity and relation extraction tasks across various datasets, such as ACE04, ACE05, SciERC, and WLPC[10]. The performance metrics, as shown in Figure 1, indicate that DyGIE achieves the highest entity and relation scores compared to other systems across all these datasets.

![Performance Metrics by Dataset](image2)

Examining the effects of coreference and relation propagation layers, Figure 4 reveals that DyGIE without Coreference Propagation (−CorefProp) achieves the highest F1 score for relations, while the full DyGIE system achieves the highest F1 score for entities. This suggests that coreference propagation significantly enhances relation extraction accuracy.

![Coreference and Relation Propagation Effects](image6)

Further analysis using Figure 6 illustrates how the number of iterations in coreference and relation propagation affects the F1 scores. For entity extraction, the best performance is achieved at two iterations of CorefProp, whereas for relation extraction, the optimal F1 score is also achieved after two iterations of RelProp. This iterative approach optimizes the extraction accuracy for both entities and relations.

question: How does the performance of the DyGIE system compare across different datasets, and what impact does coreference and relation propagation have on its entity and relation extraction tasks?
answer:
The DyGIE system demonstrates substantial improvements in both entity recognition and relation extraction across different datasets, including ACE05 and SciERC. These improvements are observed even in the absence of "gold" entity labels, which highlights the robustness of the system.

Regarding the impact of coreference and relation propagation, the results indicate that coreference propagation significantly enhances entity extraction performance, while relation propagation has a more pronounced effect on relation extraction. For instance, in the SciERC dataset, coreference propagation leads to better entity extraction performance, as shown in Table 7 where the DyGIE system achieves higher F1 scores compared to when coreference propagation is disabled.

Overall, the DyGIE system's multi-task approach, which integrates entity, relation, and coreference tasks, reduces cascading errors and leverages cross-sentence relations through coreference links, resulting in superior performance compared to previous models in scientific information extraction.

The nodes in the graph are dynam- ically selected from a beam of highly-conﬁdent mentions, and the edges are weighted according to the conﬁdence scores of relation types or coref- erences. question: How does the DyGIE model's performance on entity and relation extraction vary across different datasets and configurations, and what role do the CorefProp and RelProp components play in these variations?
answer:
The DyGIE model demonstrates substantial improvements in entity and relation extraction across various datasets and configurations. Specifically, it achieves better performance compared to previous state-of-the-art systems without relying on hand-engineered features or pipeline processing. The model's effectiveness is evident in its ability to handle cross-sentence coreference linking and reduce cascading errors between tasks.

The CorefProp component plays a crucial role in enhancing the model's performance by propagating coreference links. This propagation significantly improves the quality of automatic constructions, as shown in human evaluations. By leveraging coreference information, the model can better track entities across sentences, leading to more accurate predictions of span boundaries.

Similarly, the RelProp component contributes to the model's success by optimizing relation extraction. It helps in capturing cross-sentence relations through coreference links, which enhances the overall accuracy of relation extraction tasks. The combination of these components allows DyGIE to outperform previous models, achieving notable improvements in both entity recognition and relation extraction across different datasets and domains.

In summary, the CorefProp and RelProp components are integral to DyGIE's performance, as they facilitate better handling of coreference and relation extraction tasks, ultimately leading to improved results in scientific information extraction.

question: How does the presence of coreference annotations in datasets influence the performance of the DyGIE model in entity recognition tasks across different datasets?
answer:
The presence of coreference annotations in datasets significantly enhances the performance of the DyGIE model in entity recognition tasks across different datasets. This is evident from the results presented in Table 7, where the inclusion of coreference propagation (DYGIE-CorefProp) leads to substantial improvements in entity extraction performance on pronouns compared to the baseline model without coreference propagation (DYGIE). Specifically, the F1 score for entity recognition increases from 68.2 to 73.2 when coreference propagation is included, demonstrating the positive impact of coreference annotations on the model's ability to accurately identify and cluster entities.

Moreover, the analysis in Document 5 highlights that knowledge learned from one task, such as coreference resolution, can benefit another task like entity recognition. By leveraging coreference information, the DyGIE model is able to refine its shared span representations, leading to better performance in entity recognition. This effect is further supported by the fact that datasets with coreference annotations, such as OntoNotes, provide a richer context for training the model, resulting in improved performance across various domains and datasets.

In summary, the inclusion of coreference annotations in datasets allows the DyGIE model to achieve higher accuracy in entity recognition tasks by utilizing the additional contextual information provided by coreference links. This improvement is consistent across different datasets and domains, underscoring the importance of coreference annotations in enhancing the model's overall performance.

question: How do SWEM and CNN models compare in terms of performance across different datasets and subspace dimensions, and what insights can be drawn from their respective accuracies?
answer:
Based on the context provided, SWEM and CNN models exhibit different performance characteristics across various datasets and subspace dimensions. Here's a detailed comparison:

1. **Performance Across Datasets**:
   - On most datasets (excluding WikiQA), SWEM demonstrates superior performance compared to CNN or LSTM encoders. This suggests that SWEM is particularly effective in capturing semantic features for sentence matching tasks like natural language inference, answer sentence selection, and paraphrase identification.
   - Notably, on the SNLI dataset, SWEM-max performs the best among all SWEM variants. This aligns with findings from previous studies that max-pooling over BiLSTM hidden units outperforms average pooling on this dataset.

2. **Subspace Dimensions**:
   - SWEM shows significantly higher accuracy than CNN across a large range of low subspace dimensions. This indicates that SWEM is more parameter-efficient, achieving decent solutions with fewer parameters.
   - In contrast, CNN can leverage more trainable parameters to achieve higher accuracy when the subspace dimension is large. This suggests that CNN might be better suited for tasks requiring more complex feature extraction as the dimensionality increases.

3. **Insights from Accuracies**:
   - The effectiveness of simple pooling operations like those used in SWEM highlights their capability in representing longer documents efficiently. This makes SWEM particularly suitable for tasks involving extensive text sequences.
   - Despite its simplicity, SWEM achieves comparable or even superior results to more complex models like CNN and LSTM in sentiment analysis tasks. This underscores the importance of word-order features in sentiment analysis, where SWEM's hierarchical pooling layer effectively captures these nuances.
   - The complementary nature of SWEM-aver and SWEM-max variants, which account for different types of information from text sequences, further enhances SWEM's adaptability and robustness across various NLP tasks.

In summary, SWEM excels in scenarios requiring parameter efficiency and simpler feature extraction, while CNN tends to perform better with larger subspace dimensions and more complex feature requirements. These insights guide the rational selection of compositional functions based on the specific needs of distinct problems.

Speciﬁcally, we consider 17 datasets, including three distinct NLP tasks:  doc- ument classiﬁcation  (Yahoo news, Yelp reviews, etc .),  natural language sequence matching  (SNLI, WikiQA,  etc .) and  (short) sentence classiﬁca- tion/tagging  (Stanford sentiment treebank, TREC, etc .). Surprisingly, SWEMs exhibit comparable or even superior performance in the majority of cases considered.

Many deep learning architectures have been proposed to model the  composition- ality  in text sequences, requiring a sub- stantial number of parameters and ex- pensive computations. However, there has not been a rigorous evaluation re- garding the added value of sophisticated compositional functions. In this paper, we conduct a point-by-point comparative study between Simple Word-Embedding- based Models (SWEMs), consisting of parameter-free pooling operations, rela- tive to word-embedding-based RNN/CNN models. Surprisingly, SWEMs exhibit comparable or even superior performance in the majority of cases considered. Based upon this understanding, we propose two additional pooling strategies over learned word embeddings: ( i ) a max-pooling operation for improved interpret ability; and   $(i i)$   a hierarchical pooling operation, which preserves spatial (  $\cdot_{n}$  -gram) informa- tion within text sequences. We present experiments on 17 datasets encompassing three tasks: ( i ) (long) document classiﬁ- cation;   $(i i)$   text sequence matching; and ( iii ) short text tasks, including classiﬁca- tion and tagging.

We begin with the task of categorizing documents (with approximately 100 words in average per document). We follow the data split in  Zhang et al. ( 2015b ) for comparability. question: How does the TRADE model's performance compare across different domains when evaluated on the MultiWOZ dataset, and how does it perform in zero-shot settings?
answer:
The TRADE model demonstrates state-of-the-art performance across different domains when evaluated on the MultiWOZ dataset, achieving a joint goal accuracy of 48.62% for the five domains included in the dataset. This performance highlights its ability to effectively track dialogue states and manage complex multi-domain conversations.

In zero-shot settings, where the model encounters domains it has not seen during training, TRADE shows significant adaptability. It achieves a joint goal accuracy of 60.58% in one of the zero-shot domains, showcasing its capability to generalize knowledge from previously seen domains to new ones. Additionally, TRADE can adapt to few-shot domains without forgetting previously learned information, further emphasizing its robust transferring ability. This makes it particularly effective in handling unseen slot values and adapting to new domains with minimal additional training data.

question: How do fine-tuning strategies like GEM and EWC compare in adapting the model to new domain data, and how do slot similarities affect performance?
answer:
Fine-tuning strategies like Gradient Episodic Memory (GEM) and Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) are both designed to help models adapt to new domain data while minimizing catastrophic forgetting of previously learned information. However, they approach this challenge in different ways.

**Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC):**  
EWC uses the diagonal of the Fisher Information Matrix as a regularizer to preserve important parameters from the source domain when fine-tuning on target domain data. This matrix approximates how sensitive the model's performance is to changes in specific parameters. By penalizing large updates to these critical parameters, EWC ensures that the model retains knowledge from the source domain while adapting to the new domain. This method is particularly useful when the model needs to maintain performance across multiple domains without retraining on all previous data.

**Gradient Episodic Memory (GEM):**  
GEM, on the other hand, focuses on constraining the gradient updates during fine-tuning to ensure that the model does not forget previously learned tasks. It achieves this by storing a small set of representative examples from the source domain and using them to project the gradient updates into a subspace that preserves the performance on those examples. This allows the model to adapt to new domain data while still maintaining its ability to perform well on the original domain.

**Slot Similarities and Performance:**  
In the context of Multi-domain Wizard-of-Oz (MultiWOZ), which contains 30 domain-slot pairs and over 4,500 possible values, slot similarities play a crucial role in determining the effectiveness of these fine-tuning strategies. When slots from different domains share similar semantics or structures, the model can more easily transfer knowledge between domains. For example, if two domains have slots related to "restaurant" and "cafe," the model might benefit from shared representations that capture common attributes like location, cuisine type, or reservation options.

However, if the slots are highly dissimilar, the model may struggle to generalize across domains, leading to poorer performance. In such cases, the fine-tuning strategies need to be more carefully tuned to balance the preservation of domain-specific knowledge with the ability to adapt to new domain data. GEM and EWC both address this challenge, but their effectiveness depends on the degree of similarity between the slots and the complexity of the domains involved.

In summary, EWC and GEM offer complementary approaches to fine-tuning for multi-domain adaptation. EWC focuses on preserving important parameters from the source domain, while GEM ensures that the model does not forget previously learned tasks by constraining gradient updates. The success of these strategies in handling slot similarities depends on the extent to which the slots and domains share common characteristics, with greater similarity generally leading to better performance.

question: How do the translation accuracy and gender bias compare across different machine translation systems and languages?
answer:
Based on the context provided, there are several key points regarding translation accuracy and gender bias across different machine translation systems and languages:

1. **Translation Accuracy**:
   - The academic models, such as those by Ott et al. (2018) and Edunov et al. (2018), which are part of the WMT'14 and WMT'18 competitions respectively, show high performance in English-to-French and English-to-German translations.
   - Commercial systems like Google Translate also exhibit significant performance improvements when dealing with specific language pairs, such as Spanish, Russian, and Ukrainian.

2. **Gender Bias**:
   - The context highlights that certain portions of the WinoMT dataset (stereotypical vs. non-stereotypical) reveal varying levels of gender bias in translations. For instance, the stereotypical portion tends to perform better than the non-stereotypical portion, indicating a potential bias towards traditional gender roles.
   - Adding a gender feature to NMT systems has shown to significantly improve translation quality for some languages, reducing bias notably in Spanish, Russian, and Ukrainian.

3. **System Comparisons**:
   - The commercial MT systems tested generally display similar trends in terms of bias and accuracy, suggesting that while they may have advanced capabilities, they still retain biases present in their training data.
   - Academic models seem to handle these issues more effectively, potentially due to their focus on specific research challenges and innovative approaches.

4. **Language-Specific Insights**:
   - Languages like Spanish, Russian, and Ukrainian show notable improvements in reducing gender bias when using enhanced models or datasets that incorporate gender-specific information.
   - The effectiveness of these improvements varies, indicating that while progress is being made, there is still room for further refinement in addressing gender bias in machine translation.

In summary, while there have been advancements in both translation accuracy and efforts to mitigate gender bias, the performance and bias levels can vary significantly depending on the system used and the specific language pair involved. Continued research and development in this area aim to further enhance fairness and accuracy in machine translation systems.

The translation accuracy and gender bias across different machine translation (MT) systems and languages exhibit significant variations. This analysis draws upon several metrics including accuracy percentage (Acc), and gender bias indicators such as Δ_G and Δ_S[5]. 

### Comparison by Translation Systems and Languages

- **Google Translate** shows high accuracy for French (FR) with 63.6% but exhibits large Δ_G variations, notably in Arabic (AR) with 43.7. The Δ_S metric is also variable, with Hebrew (HE) showing a noticeable change (37.8).

- **Microsoft Translator** achieves the highest accuracy with German (DE) at 74.1%. Δ_G scores are particularly high for AR at 48.3, indicating significant grammatical changes. Δ_S shows considerable change in DE with 30.2.

- **Amazon Translate** performs best for Spanish (ES) with 59.4% accuracy. Δ_G scores are consistent, with AR being most affected at 38.5. Notable Δ_S changes are seen in HE with 47.3.

- **SYSTRAN** achieves higher accuracy for DE at 48.6%. Significant Δ_G changes occur across languages, especially AR with 49.4, while Δ_S is stable, with HE exhibiting higher alterations at 24.5.

These metrics demonstrate the performance variations among translation services for each language, reflecting how each service manages grammatical and semantic changes differently.

![Figure 1](image2)

### Gender Bias in Translation

The accuracy in translating gender-related content also varies between stereotypical and non-stereotypical translations:

![Figure 3](image3)

- **Stereotypical translations** consistently show higher accuracy. For example, French (FR) has an accuracy rate of 80% for stereotypical translations compared to 54% for non-stereotypical ones.

- This trend is visible across all tested languages, indicating a bias towards more traditional gender roles in translations[1].

In conclusion, both accuracy and gender bias metrics reveal that machine translation systems handle different languages with varied effectiveness, and there is a notable bias in translating gender-related content, favoring stereotypical representations. These findings highlight the need for continued improvement in MT systems to address these biases and enhance accuracy across languages.

We present the ﬁrst challenge set and eval- uation protocol for the analysis of gender bias in machine translation (MT). Our ap- proach uses two recent coreference resolution datasets composed of English sentences which cast participants into non-stereotypical gender roles (e.g., “The doctor asked the nurse to help her  in the operation”). We devise an automatic gender bias evaluation method for eight tar- get languages with grammatical gender, based on morphological analysis (e.g., the use of fe- male inﬂection for the word “doctor”). Our analyses show that four popular industrial MT systems and two recent state-of-the-art aca- demic MT models are signiﬁcantly prone to gender-biased translation errors for all tested target languages. Our data and code are pub- licly available at  https://github.com/ gabriel St a nov sky/mt_gender .

We estimate the accuracy of our gender bias evalu- ation method by randomly sampling 100 instances of all translation systems and target languages, an- notating each sample by two target-language na- tive speakers (resulting in 9,600 human annota- tions). Each instance conformed to a format sim- ilar to that used by our automatic gender detec- tion algorithm: human annotators were asked to mark the gender of an entity within a given target- language sentence. question: How do stereotype-based adjustments in machine translation impact gender bias accuracy across different languages?
answer:
Based on the context provided, stereotype-based adjustments in machine translation (MT) significantly impact gender bias accuracy across different languages. The studies show that when MT systems are presented with pro-stereotypical gender role assignments (e.g., a female nurse), their performance is consistently better compared to anti-stereotypical roles (e.g., a male receptionist). This trend is observed across multiple languages, including Spanish, Russian, and Ukrainian.

The introduction of stereotypical gender adjectives in the dataset appears to improve the accuracy of gender predictions for these languages. For instance, Table 4 from Document 3 highlights the performance improvements in Google Translate for Spanish, Russian, and Ukrainian when using a modified version of the WinoMT corpus that includes stereotypical gender adjectives. The accuracy increases notably in each case, suggesting that aligning translations with societal stereotypes can reduce perceived gender bias in MT outputs.

However, it's important to note that while these adjustments may improve accuracy in certain contexts, they also risk reinforcing existing gender stereotypes. The approach assumes oracle coreference resolution and serves as an indication of the relationship between coreference resolution and MT, but it is not a practical general debiasing scheme. The findings underscore the complex interplay between gender bias, coreference resolution, and MT performance, highlighting the need for more nuanced strategies to address gender bias in machine translation effectively.
reference_answer_short: Stereotype-based adjustments improve gender bias accuracy by aligning gender-specific adjectives with the correct pronouns, reducing inaccuracies in translations.
reference_answers:
Stereotype-based adjustments in machine translation can significantly impact accuracy regarding gender bias by aligning gender-specific adjectives with the correct pronouns, thus reducing translation inaccuracies[4]. 

For instance, in Figure 5, we see how adding a stereotypically female adjective, such as 'pretty', corrects the translation by aligning the gender of the noun with the pronoun. Originally, 'baker' was translated into 'el panadero', a male inflection, which mismatched with the female pronoun 'ella'. After the adjustment, it became 'la panadera bonita', properly matching the gender.

![Translation Examples](image3)

Similarly, Figure 4 illustrates that stereotype-based adjustments lead to improved accuracy scores across different languages. For example, Spanish (ES) translations see a jump from 53.1% to 63.5% in accuracy, Russian (RU) from 37.7% to 48.9%, and Ukrainian (UK) from 38.4% to 42.9% after adjustments[8]. This indicates that incorporating stereotypical gender roles substantially enhances translation accuracy.

![Adjustment Impact](image2)

Moreover, as displayed in Figure 3, Google's translation accuracy for stereotypical gender roles is consistently higher across all tested languages compared to non-stereotypical roles. For instance, in French (FR), the accuracy is 80% for stereotypical roles but drops to 54% for non-stereotypical ones.

![Stereotypical vs Non-Stereotypical](image1)

In conclusion, stereotype-based adjustments help correct gender biases in translations, leading to more accurate and contextually appropriate results across various languages[6]. This underscores the importance of adaptive language models that account for gender nuances in translation tasks.

question: How do different training and evaluation strategies affect F1 scores in multi-hop and single-hop question answering tasks?
answer:
The training and evaluation strategies significantly impact F1 scores in both multi-hop and single-hop question answering tasks. In the context provided, it is evident that models like BERT, which are designed for single-hop reasoning, can achieve competitive performance on datasets like HOTPOTQA, despite their inability to reason across multiple paragraphs. This suggests that many questions in such datasets can be effectively addressed using single-hop reasoning techniques.

For multi-hop reasoning tasks, datasets like MuSiQue and StrategyQA present more complex challenges. These datasets require models to integrate information from multiple sources or pieces of evidence to arrive at an answer. The experiments with models like PaLM-2L and GPT-4 indicate that while these large language models (LLMs) can handle such tasks, they often necessitate specific strategies or additional computational resources.

Evaluation metrics also play a crucial role. Traditional metrics like accuracy and F1 score have limitations when assessing the performance of state-of-the-art LLMs, especially when dealing with long-form answers. The use of a few-shot prompting approach with models like PaLM2-L helps in better capturing the equivalence between target answers and model predictions, providing a more nuanced evaluation.

In summary, the choice of model architecture, the complexity of the dataset, and the evaluation strategy all contribute to the F1 scores observed in these tasks. Single-hop models can perform well on datasets where questions can be answered with a single piece of evidence, while multi-hop tasks require more sophisticated models and strategies to achieve high F1 scores.
reference_answer_short: Adversarial training improves performance on adversarial evaluation data compared to original training, while single-paragraph models struggle with open-domain settings.
reference_answers:
To understand the impact of different training and evaluation strategies on F1 scores in question answering tasks, we can analyze the provided data from the tables and descriptions.

The analysis focuses on the influence of adversarial training and evaluation in multi-hop and single-hop scenarios.

First, let's consider the performance metrics for different combinations of training and evaluation data:

![F1 Scores for Different Training and Evaluation Combinations](image4)

- **Original Training Data**: When evaluated on original data, this yields a high F1 score of 67.08. However, performance drops significantly to 46.84 when evaluated on adversarial data, highlighting the model's vulnerability to adversarial examples.
- **Adversarial Training Data**: This training strategy improves the model's robustness, as seen by an F1 score of 60.10 on adversarial evaluation data, a significant improvement over using original training data[6]. When evaluated on original data, the adversarially trained model scores 59.12, indicating a trade-off in generalizability.
- **Adversarial + Type Evaluation**: Adding entity type information improves the adversarially trained model's performance further to an F1 score of 58.42[6], suggesting benefits from more nuanced training data.

In terms of open-domain settings, the F1 scores are shown below:

![F1 Scores for Open-domain and Distractor Settings](image2)

- **Distractor Setting**: The model achieves an F1 score of 67.08, indicating strong performance when the task involves distractor paragraphs.
- **Open-domain 10 Paragraphs**: Here, the F1 score drops to 38.40, showcasing the challenges of open-domain questions that require broader context.
- **Open-domain 500 Paragraphs**: Marginal improvement to 39.12 suggests that simply increasing the number of paragraphs does not significantly enhance performance.
- **Open-domain with Gold Paragraph**: Adding a gold paragraph boosts the F1 score to 53.12[6], underscoring the importance of high-quality, relevant information in improving model accuracy.

Overall, adversarial training enhances the model's ability to handle adversarial examples, while a gold paragraph significantly aids performance in open-domain settings. This analysis highlights the importance of robust training strategies and the inclusion of quality context in improving question answering models across various scenarios.

question: How does the adversarial data setup affect the performance of BERT models on the ARCT dataset, and what conclusions can be drawn from such results?
answer:
The adversarial data setup significantly impacts the performance of BERT models on the ARCT dataset. According to the context, BERT's peak performance drops from around 71% accuracy to approximately 50%, with both mean and median accuracy falling below 53%. This indicates that the adversarial setup effectively eliminates the spurious statistical cues that BERT was previously exploiting, leading to a more robust evaluation of its true capabilities in argument comprehension.

From these results, we can conclude that BERT's high performance on the original dataset was largely due to its ability to exploit superficial patterns rather than understanding the underlying logic of arguments. The adversarial setup forces the model to rely on genuine comprehension skills, revealing that BERT has not truly learned how to comprehend arguments but instead relies on statistical shortcuts. This suggests that future evaluations of machine learning models should incorporate adversarial testing to ensure they are genuinely capable of handling complex reasoning tasks rather than simply leveraging biases in the training data.
reference_answer_short: The adversarial setup reduces BERT's performance, highlighting the exploitation of spurious cues in the original data. It shows BERT's reliance on superficial cues rather than deeper reasoning.
reference_answers:
The adversarial data setup significantly impacts the performance of BERT models on the ARCT dataset, as illustrated by the results in the provided figures and screenshots.

In the original setup, BERT was able to achieve relatively high performance metrics. However, when subjected to the adversarial dataset, as shown in Table 4 from the document (extracted as figure 2)[1], the performance of the BERT models dropped substantially. The mean performance for the standard BERT model on the adversarial test set was 0.504, with a median of 0.505 and a maximum of 0.533. This is a stark contrast to the original setup where BERT achieved much higher scores, indicating the detrimental impact of the adversarial setup.

![Performance Metrics for BERT Models](image4)

The adversarial data setup involves reversing the logic of claims and warrants, as demonstrated in the comparison table (extracted as figure 1). This setup effectively nullifies the superficial statistical cues that BERT models might exploit in the original dataset, such as strong signal words or phrases that do not require deep understanding or reasoning to interpret correctly.

![Original vs. Adversarial Data Points](image3)

From these results, it can be concluded that BERT's performance is heavily reliant on these superficial cues, as the adversarial setup, which removes these cues, results in a performance drop to near random levels[3][6][3][8]. This suggests that BERT, while powerful, may not be engaging in genuine understanding or reasoning, but rather exploiting statistical regularities present in the data.

The findings emphasize the necessity for models to develop deeper reasoning capabilities and to be tested on datasets that truly challenge these abilities, free from spurious statistical cues. This approach not only provides a more realistic evaluation of machine comprehension but also aligns with the goal of developing models that can handle complex reasoning tasks effectively.
